questions.text: Explain the divisor method to find GCD of 18 and 24.
questions.answer: List all divisors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. List all divisors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. The common divisors are 1, 2, 3, 6. The greatest among them is 6, so GCD is 6.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Find the LCM of 6 and 8 using the listing method.
questions.answer: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, ... Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, ... The common multiples are 24, 48, ... The smallest common multiple is 24. Hence, LCM is 24.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is 1 not considered a prime number?
questions.answer: A prime number must have exactly two distinct factors. The number 1 has only one factor, which is itself. Therefore, it does not meet the criteria for a prime number.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: How do you find the GCD using prime factorisation? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: Write the prime factorisation of each number. Identify the common prime factors. Multiply these common factors to get the GCD. For example, for 24 (2×2×2×3) and 36 (2×2×3×3), common factors are 2, 2, 3. So GCD = 2×2×3 = 12.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the LCM of two co-prime numbers equal to their product?
questions.answer: Co-prime numbers have no common prime factors. Therefore, their LCM must include all prime factors from both numbers. Since there is no overlap, the LCM is simply the product of the two numbers.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the GCD of two numbers always a divisor of their LCM?
questions.answer: The GCD contains only the common prime factors of the two numbers. The LCM contains all prime factors of both numbers, including those in the GCD. Hence, the GCD divides the LCM.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why do we use LCM to find when two events will happen together again?
questions.answer: LCM gives the smallest time interval that is a multiple of the individual periods of the events. At this time, both events complete an integer number of cycles and occur simultaneously.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the relationship between GCD and LCM of two numbers with an example.
questions.answer: The product of two numbers is equal to the product of their GCD and LCM. For example, take 12 and 18. GCD(12, 18) = 6, LCM(12, 18) = 36. Product of numbers: 12 × 18 = 216. Product of GCD and LCM: 6 × 36 = 216. Hence, 12 × 18 = GCD × LCM. This relationship holds for any pair of natural numbers and is useful in solving problems where one of GCD or LCM is unknown.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the prime factorisation method to find LCM of 12, 18 and 30.
questions.answer: First, find the prime factors of each number: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3, 18 = 2 × 3 × 3, 30 = 2 × 3 × 5. For LCM, take the highest power of each prime factor present in any number. Prime 2 appears at most twice (in 12), prime 3 appears at most twice (in 18), prime 5 appears once (in 30). So LCM = 2² × 3² × 5 = 4 × 9 × 5 = 180. Thus, LCM of 12, 18 and 30 is 180. This method ensures the smallest number divisible by all.

questions.text: Find the GCD of 48 and 60 using the division method.
questions.answer: 60 ÷ 48 = 1 remainder 12 48 ÷ 12 = 4 remainder 0 Since remainder is 0, the last divisor is 12. Hence, GCD of 48 and 60 is 12.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: The length and breadth of a rectangular floor are 18 m and 24 m. Find the maximum size of square tile that can be used to cover the floor without cutting.
questions.answer: We need to find GCD of 18 and 24. Divisors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18 Divisors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 Common divisors: 1, 2, 3, 6 Greatest common divisor = 6 Hence, maximum size of square tile = 6 m.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Three bells ring at intervals of 6, 8 and 12 minutes. If they ring together at 9:00 AM, after how many minutes will they ring together again?
questions.answer: Find LCM of 6, 8 and 12. Prime factors: 6 = 2 × 3 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 Take highest powers: 2³ and 3¹ LCM = 2³ × 3 = 8 × 3 = 24 Hence, they will ring together again after 24 minutes.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: The product of two numbers is 168 and their GCD is 4. Find their LCM.
questions.answer: We know: Product of numbers = GCD × LCM So, 168 = 4 × LCM Therefore, LCM = 168 ÷ 4 = 42 Hence, LCM is 42.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Find the smallest number that is divisible by both 15 and 20.
questions.answer: We need LCM of 15 and 20. Prime factors: 15 = 3 × 5 20 = 2 × 2 × 5 Take highest powers: 2², 3, 5 LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 Hence, the smallest number divisible by both 15 and 20 is 60.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Two ropes are 24 cm and 36 cm long. They are to be cut into pieces of equal maximum length. What is the length of each piece?
questions.answer: We need GCD of 24 and 36. Prime factors: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 Common factors: 2, 2, 3 GCD = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 Hence, each piece will be 12 cm long.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain how to check if two fractions are equivalent.
questions.answer: Two fractions are equivalent if their cross products are equal. For example, to check 2/3 and 4/6, multiply 2×6 and 3×4; both give 12, so they are equivalent. Alternatively, simplify both fractions to their lowest terms and see if they match.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: How do you add two unlike fractions?
questions.answer: To add unlike fractions, first find the LCM of the denominators. Then convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with the LCM as the denominator. Finally, add the numerators and keep the common denominator.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: What is a mixed fraction? Give an example.
questions.answer: A mixed fraction consists of a whole number and a proper fraction. For example, 2 1/3 is a mixed fraction where 2 is the whole part and 1/3 is the fractional part.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is 5/5 considered an improper fraction?

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is 3/4 greater than 2/3?
questions.answer: To compare 3/4 and 2/3, we make the denominators equal. The LCM of 4 and 3 is 12. Converting, 3/4 becomes 9/12 and 2/3 becomes 8/12. Since 9/12 > 8/12, therefore 3/4 > 2/3.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why must we find the LCM when adding or subtracting unlike fractions?
questions.answer: We find the LCM to make the denominators the same so that the fractions represent parts of the same-sized whole. Only then can we add or subtract the numerators meaningfully.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the fraction 0/7 equal to zero?

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the concept of fractions with the help of an activity involving paper folding.
questions.answer: Take a rectangular sheet of paper. Fold it into two equal parts and shade one part; this represents 1/2. Fold it again into two equal parts (now four parts) and shade one part; this shows 1/4. Continue folding to get 1/8, 1/16, etc. Each fold divides the existing parts into two equal halves, demonstrating how fractions represent equal parts of a whole. This activity helps visualize that as the denominator increases, the size of each part decreases. It also shows equivalent fractions: for example, shading two parts out of four (2/4) is the same as shading one part out of two (1/2).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe how to compare fractions using a number line.
questions.answer: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Divide the segment between 0 and 1 into equal parts based on the denominator of the fractions. For example, to compare 1/3 and 2/5, first find a common denominator or estimate. Mark 1/3 by dividing the line into 3 parts and taking the first mark. Mark 2/5 by dividing into 5 parts and taking the second. The fraction corresponding to the point farther to the right is larger. Since 2/5 (0.4) lies to the right of 1/3 (≈0.33), 2/5 > 1/3. This method works well for visual comparison.

questions.answer: The unitary method is a technique to find the value of a single unit and then use it to find the value of multiple units.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain how to find the ratio of 5 years to 10 months in simplest form.
questions.answer: First convert 5 years to months: 5 × 12 = 60 months. Then form the ratio 60:10. Simplify by dividing both by 10: 6:1. Hence, the simplest form is 6:1.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: In a class of 45 students, 15 play hockey, 20 play kabaddi, and the rest play kho-kho. Find the ratio of students playing kho-kho to total students.
questions.answer: Number of kho-kho players = 45 - (15 + 20) = 10. Ratio of kho-kho to total = 10:45. Simplify by dividing by 5: 2:9.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: The length of a rectangular sheet is 1.20 m and width is 48 cm. Find the ratio of width to length.
questions.answer: Convert length to cm: 1.20 m = 120 cm. Width = 48 cm. Ratio = 48:120. Simplify by dividing by 24: 2:5.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: If 12 pencils cost Rs. 144, how much will 10 pencils cost using the unitary method?
questions.answer: Cost of 1 pencil = 144 ÷ 12 = Rs. 12. Cost of 10 pencils = 10 × 12 = Rs. 120.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the ratio of 2 kg to 800 grams equal to 5:2?
questions.answer: First convert 2 kg to grams: 2 × 1000 = 2000 grams. Then the ratio is 2000:800. Divide both by 400: 5:2. Hence, the ratio is 5:2.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain why the ratio of length to width remains the same when a photograph is resized proportionally.
questions.answer: When a photograph is resized proportionally, both length and width are multiplied or divided by the same factor. Since the same factor applies to both, their ratio remains unchanged.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why does a ratio have no unit?
questions.answer: A ratio is a comparison of two quantities of the same kind, so the units cancel out during division, leaving a unitless number.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the concept of ratio and proportion with two examples from daily life.
questions.answer: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, showing how many times one contains the other. It is written in simplest form. Proportion states that two ratios are equal. Example 1: In a recipe, 2 cups of flour to 1 cup of sugar gives ratio 2:1. If doubled, it becomes 4:2, which is proportional. Example 2: A map scale of 1 cm = 10 km means ratio 1:100000. If two cities are 5 cm apart on map, actual distance is 5 × 10 = 50 km.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the unitary method and solve: If 5 notebooks cost Rs. 75, what is the cost of 8 notebooks?
questions.answer: The unitary method involves finding the value of one unit first, then scaling up or down. Cost of 5 notebooks = Rs. 75. So, cost of 1 notebook = 75 ÷ 5 = Rs. 15. Therefore, cost of 8 notebooks = 8 × 15 = Rs. 120. This method is useful in problems involving cost, distance, time, etc., where direct proportion exists.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Suresh walks 1700 meters every morning, while his friend Ramesh walks 2 kilometers every day. Find the ratio of the distance covered by Suresh to the distance covered by Ramesh in simplest form.
questions.answer: Convert Ramesh's distance to meters: 2 km = 2 × 1000 = 2000 m. Now, ratio = 1700 : 2000 Divide both by 100: 17 : 20 Since 17 and 20 have no common factor other than 1, the simplest form is 17:20.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: In a factory, 320 workers are employed. Out of them, 200 are male. Find the ratio of male workers to female workers and male workers to total workers.
questions.answer: Number of female workers = 320 - 200 = 120 Ratio of male to female = 200 : 120 Divide by 40: 5 : 3 Ratio of male to total = 200 : 320 Divide by 40: 5 : 8 Hence, male : female = 5:3 and male : total = 5:8.

questions.text: A goods train covers 240 km in 4 hours. How far will it go in 7 hours at the same speed?
questions.answer: Distance in 4 hours = 240 km Distance in 1 hour = 240 ÷ 4 = 60 km Distance in 7 hours = 60 × 7 = 420 km Hence, the train will cover 420 km in 7 hours.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Anil built a 50 feet long wall using 10 bags of cement. Sandeep built a 25 feet long wall using 5 bags. Are the length of wall and cement used in proportion?
questions.answer: Ratio of length (Anil:Sandeep) = 50:25 = 2:1 Ratio of cement bags (Anil:Sandeep) = 10:5 = 2:1 Since both ratios are equal, the length of wall and cement used are in proportion.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the types of triangles based on sides with examples.
questions.answer: Triangles based on sides are: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (any two sides equal), and scalene (all sides unequal). For example, an equilateral triangle has all sides 5 cm, isosceles has two sides 5 cm and base 3 cm, scalene has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why can a triangle not have two right angles?
questions.answer: A triangle cannot have two right angles because the sum of angles in a triangle is 180°. If two angles are 90° each, their sum is already 180°, leaving 0° for the third angle, which is impossible.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is an equilateral triangle always an acute angled triangle?
questions.answer: An equilateral triangle has all sides equal, so all angles are equal. Since the sum of angles is 180°, each angle is 60°, which is less than 90°. Hence, all angles are acute, making it an acute angled triangle.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why do we say that a quadrilateral has two diagonals?
questions.answer: A quadrilateral has four vertices. A diagonal joins opposite vertices. There are two pairs of opposite vertices: (A,C) and (B,D) in quadrilateral ABCD. Hence, there are two diagonals: AC and BD.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the types of triangles based on sides and angles. Give one example each.
questions.answer: Triangles are classified based on sides into equilateral, isosceles, and scalene. Based on angles, they are acute angled, right angled, and obtuse angled. An equilateral triangle has all sides equal and each angle 60°, so it is also acute angled. An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and can be acute, right, or obtuse angled depending on the angle between equal sides. A scalene triangle has all sides unequal and can belong to any angle-based type. For example, a triangle with sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm is isosceles and acute angled; one with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm is scalene and right angled.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the elements of a quadrilateral: sides, angles, vertices, diagonals, adjacent and opposite sides and angles.
questions.answer: A quadrilateral has four vertices, four sides, four angles, and two diagonals. Adjacent sides share a common vertex; there are four such pairs. Opposite sides do not meet; there are two pairs. Similarly, adjacent angles share a common side (four pairs), while opposite angles do not share a side (two pairs). Diagonals join opposite vertices. For example, in quadrilateral PQRS, sides PQ and QR are adjacent, while PQ and RS are opposite. Angles ∠PQR and ∠QRS are adjacent, while ∠PQR and ∠PSR are opposite. The diagonals are PR and QS.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: The sides of a triangle are 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm. Check if it is a right angled triangle.
questions.answer: To check if the triangle is right angled, we use Pythagoras theorem: (hypotenuse)² = (base)² + (height)². Longest side = 10 cm. (10)² = 100. (6)² + (8)² = 36 + 64 = 100. Since 100 = 100, the triangle satisfies Pythagoras theorem. Hence, it is a right angled triangle.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. Find the third angle.
questions.answer: Sum of angles in a triangle = 180°. Sum of given angles = 50° + 60° = 110°. Third angle = 180° – 110° = 70°. Hence, the third angle is 70°.

questions.text: In an isosceles triangle, the equal sides are 5 cm each and the base is 6 cm. Find the perimeter.
questions.answer: Perimeter = sum of all sides = 5 cm + 5 cm + 6 cm = 16 cm. Hence, the perimeter is 16 cm.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:4. Find the angles.
questions.answer: Let the angles be 2x, 3x, 4x. Sum = 2x + 3x + 4x = 9x = 180°. So, x = 180° / 9 = 20°. Angles: 2x = 40°, 3x = 60°, 4x = 80°. Hence, the angles are 40°, 60°, and 80°.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A quadrilateral has three angles equal to 80°, 100°, and 120°. Find the fourth angle.
questions.answer: Sum of angles in a quadrilateral = 360°. Sum of given angles = 80° + 100° + 120° = 300°. Fourth angle = 360° – 300° = 60°. Hence, the fourth angle is 60°.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 24 cm. Find the length of each side.
questions.answer: Perimeter = 3 × side. So, side = Perimeter / 3 = 24 / 3 = 8 cm. Hence, each side is 8 cm long.

questions.text: Why is the solution of 0 × x = 0 not unique?

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the concept of an equation in one variable with an example. Describe how to find its solution using the properties of equality.
questions.answer: An equation in one variable is a mathematical statement that shows two expressions are equal, and it contains only one unknown number represented by a letter. For example, x + 5 = 12 is an equation in one variable x. To find the solution, we use the properties of equality to isolate the variable. Subtract 5 from both sides: x + 5 - 5 = 12 - 5, which gives x = 7. We check by substituting: 7 + 5 = 12, which is true. Hence, x = 7 is the solution. This process works because adding or subtracting the same number from both sides does not change the equality.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Solve the equation 3x - 4 = 11 step by step and explain each step using the properties of equality.
questions.answer: Start with the equation: 3x - 4 = 11. First, add 4 to both sides to undo the subtraction: 3x - 4 + 4 = 11 + 4, which simplifies to 3x = 15. This uses the addition property of equality. Next, divide both sides by 3 to isolate x: 3x ÷ 3 = 15 ÷ 3, which gives x = 5. This uses the division property of equality. Finally, check the solution: substitute x = 5 into the original equation: 3 × 5 - 4 = 15 - 4 = 11, which matches the right side. Hence, x = 5 is the correct solution.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Solve the equation: 2(x + 3) = 16
questions.answer: Step 1: Divide both sides by 2 (using division property of equality): (x + 3) = 8 Step 2: Subtract 3 from both sides (using subtraction property of equality): x = 8 - 3 Step 3: Simplify: x = 5 Check: Substitute x = 5 into the original equation: Left side: 2(5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 Right side: 16 Since both sides are equal, the solution is correct. Hence, x = 5.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Solve the equation: 5x - 7 = 18
questions.answer: Step 1: Add 7 to both sides (addition property of equality): 5x - 7 + 7 = 18 + 7 Step 2: Simplify: 5x = 25 Step 3: Divide both sides by 5 (division property of equality): x = 25 ÷ 5 Step 4: Simplify: x = 5 Check: Substitute x = 5: Left side: 5 × 5 - 7 = 25 - 7 = 18 Right side: 18 Both sides are equal, so the solution is correct. Hence, x = 5.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Solve the equation: x ÷ 4 + 2 = 6
questions.answer: Step 1: Subtract 2 from both sides (subtraction property of equality): x ÷ 4 + 2 - 2 = 6 - 2 Step 2: Simplify: x ÷ 4 = 4 Step 3: Multiply both sides by 4 (multiplication property of equality): x = 4 × 4 Step 4: Simplify: x = 16 Check: Substitute x = 16: Left side: 16 ÷ 4 + 2 = 4 + 2 = 6 Right side: 6 Both sides are equal, so the solution is correct. Hence, x = 16.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Solve the equation: 3x + 5 = 2x + 9
questions.answer: Step 1: Subtract 2x from both sides to get variables on one side (subtraction property): 3x - 2x + 5 = 2x - 2x + 9 Step 2: Simplify: x + 5 = 9 Step 3: Subtract 5 from both sides (subtraction property): x + 5 - 5 = 9 - 5 Step 4: Simplify: x = 4 Check: Substitute x = 4: Left side: 3 × 4 + 5 = 12 + 5 = 17 Right side: 2 × 4 + 9 = 8 + 9 = 17 Both sides are equal, so the solution is correct. Hence, x = 4.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Solve the equation: 4(x - 2) = 20
questions.answer: Step 1: Divide both sides by 4 (division property of equality): x - 2 = 20 ÷ 4 Step 2: Simplify: x - 2 = 5 Step 3: Add 2 to both sides (addition property of equality): x = 5 + 2 Step 4: Simplify: x = 7 Check: Substitute x = 7: Left side: 4(7 - 2) = 4 × 5 = 20 Right side: 20 Both sides are equal, so the solution is correct. Hence, x = 7.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Solve the equation: 7 - x = 3
questions.answer: Step 1: Add x to both sides to bring variable to one side (addition property): 7 = 3 + x Step 2: Subtract 3 from both sides (subtraction property): 7 - 3 = x Step 3: Simplify: 4 = x Or, x = 4 Check: Substitute x = 4: Left side: 7 - 4 = 3 Right side: 3 Both sides are equal, so the solution is correct. Hence, x = 4.

questions.text: Explain how the smart card trick works to guess a number between 1 and 31 using 5 cards.
questions.answer: Each card represents a binary place value (1, 2, 4, 8, 16). The number is found by adding the values of the cards that contain the chosen number. This works because every number from 1 to 31 has a unique binary representation using 5 bits.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: How can you verify that a set of pentominoes perfectly covers a 6x10 rectangle?
questions.answer: By placing all 12 pentominoes (each of area 5) without overlapping or leaving gaps, the total area covered is 12 × 5 = 60 square units, which matches the area of the 6×10 rectangle. A valid arrangement confirms perfect tessellation.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the sum of angles in a pentagon 540°?
questions.answer: A pentagon can be divided into 3 triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Since each triangle has 180°, the total is 3 × 180° = 540°.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Differentiate between a regular and an irregular pentagon.
questions.answer: A regular pentagon has all sides equal and all angles equal (each 108°). An irregular pentagon has sides and/or angles of different measures, so they are not uniform.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the sum of the angles at the points of a five-pointed star equal to 180°?
questions.answer: The angles at the points of the star are formed by the intersection of lines. By considering the triangles formed and using the exterior angle theorem or straight line properties, the sum of these five angles equals 180°, as they collectively form a straight line or relate to the internal pentagon's angle sum.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why can pentominoes be used to teach concepts of area and perimeter?
questions.answer: Each pentomino has a fixed area of 5 square units (since it's made of 5 unit squares), but different perimeters depending on shape. This helps students compare how shapes with same area can have different perimeters, reinforcing the distinction between area and perimeter.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the internal polygon in a regular star always a regular polygon?
questions.answer: When a regular star is formed by extending the sides of a regular polygon in a symmetric way, the intersection points are equidistant and symmetrically placed, resulting in a similar, smaller regular polygon at the center.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the activity of making pentominoes on grid paper and explain how it helps in understanding tessellation and area conservation.
questions.answer: Students cut out shapes made of 5 connected unit squares from grid paper, creating the 12 unique pentominoes. They then attempt to fit these pieces into rectangles like 6×10, 5×12, 4×15, or 3×20 without overlaps or gaps. This activity teaches that despite different shapes, each pentomino has the same area (5 sq units), so total area remains conserved. Successfully filling a rectangle demonstrates tessellation — covering a plane with repeating shapes. It also develops spatial reasoning, problem-solving, and an intuitive grasp of how area and shape relate.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the smart card trick with numbers 1 to 31 and how it uses binary representation to guess a number.
questions.answer: The smart card trick uses 5 cards, each containing numbers that have a specific bit set in their binary form. Card 1 has numbers with the 1s place (1,3,5,...), Card 2 has 2s place (2,3,6,7,...), and so on up to 16s place. When a friend thinks of a number, they indicate which cards contain it. The magician adds the first number (power of 2) on each selected card. This sum equals the thought number because binary representation uniquely expresses any number as a sum of powers of 2. For example, if the number is 21 (10101 in binary), it appears on cards 1, 4, and 5 (1+16+4=21). This trick demonstrates how binary coding works in a fun, engaging way.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: If each interior angle of a regular polygon is 108°, find the number of sides of the polygon.
questions.answer: Each interior angle = 108° Let number of sides = n Formula: Interior angle = [(n-2) × 180°] / n So, 108 = [(n-2) × 180] / n Multiply both sides by n: 108n = 180(n-2) 108n = 180n - 360 Bring terms together: 108n - 180n = -360 -72n = -360 Divide by -72: n = (-360) / (-72) = 5 Therefore, the polygon has 5 sides.

questions.answer: Number of sides, n = 10 Sum of interior angles = (n-2) × 180° = (10-2) × 180° = 8 × 180° = 1440° Therefore, the sum is 1440 degrees.

questions.answer: Area of rectangle = length × breadth = 5 × 12 = 60 square units Each pentomino is made of 5 unit squares → Area of one pentomino = 5 square units Number of pentominoes = Total area ÷ Area of one pentomino = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 Therefore, 12 pentominoes are used to cover 60 square units.

questions.text: If the sum of angles in a polygon is 900°, find the number of sides.
questions.answer: Sum of interior angles = (n-2) × 180° = 900° So, (n-2) × 180 = 900 Divide both sides by 180: n-2 = 900 ÷ 180 = 5 Add 2: n = 5 + 2 = 7 Therefore, the polygon has 7 sides.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: In a 5-pointed star, if one angle at the point is 30°, what is the sum of all five point angles?
questions.answer: In a 5-pointed star, regardless of individual angle measures, the sum of the angles at the five points is always 180°. This is a geometric property derived from the fact that the star can be decomposed into triangles whose external angles sum to 180°. Therefore, even if one angle is 30°, the sum of all five point angles = 180°.

questions.text: How do you compare two decimal fractions? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: First, compare the integer parts. If they are equal, compare the digits after the decimal point from left to right. For example, to compare 5.67 and 5.6, the integer parts are equal, so compare tenths: both are 6, then hundredths: 7 > 0, so 5.67 > 5.6.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why do we align decimal points while adding or subtracting decimal fractions?
questions.answer: We align decimal points to ensure that digits of the same place value (tenths, hundredths, etc.) are in the same column. This allows correct addition or subtraction of corresponding place values.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is 0.001 smaller than 0.01?
questions.answer: 0.001 represents one thousandth, while 0.01 represents one hundredth. Since one hundredth is greater than one thousandth, 0.01 > 0.001.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the uses of decimal fractions in daily life with examples.
questions.answer: Decimal fractions are used in daily life for precise measurements. For example, prices of items like ₹25.50, measurements like 1.75 metres of cloth, or weight like 0.5 kg of apples. They are used in fuel pumps to show litres filled, in thermometers to record temperature like 98.6°F, and in timers for races. Decimal fractions make calculations easy in shops, banks, and science labs where accuracy is important.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Write a short note on the place value system in decimal numbers.
questions.answer: In decimal numbers, the place value system extends to the right of the decimal point. The first place after the decimal is tenths (1/10), then hundredths (1/100), then thousandths (1/1000), and so on. Each place is one-tenth of the place to its left. For example, in 45.678, 6 is in the tenths place (0.6), 7 in hundredths (0.07), and 8 in thousandths (0.008). This system allows us to write fractions like 3/10 as 0.3 and perform arithmetic easily.

questions.text: Explain how to calculate profit or loss in a transaction with an example.
questions.answer: To calculate profit or loss, compare the selling price and cost price. If selling price > cost price, profit = selling price - cost price. If selling price < cost price, loss = cost price - selling price. For example, if cost price is ₹1000 and selling price is ₹1200, profit is ₹200.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: What is total cost price? List two examples of expenses included in it.
questions.answer: Total cost price is the sum of the original cost price and all other expenses incurred in acquiring or preparing the goods for sale. Examples of such expenses include transportation cost and wages paid to workers.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: A farmer spent ₹3000 on seeds and ₹500 on fertilizer. He sold the crop for ₹4000. Did he make a profit or loss? How much?
questions.answer: Total cost price = ₹3000 + ₹500 = ₹3500. Selling price = ₹4000. Since selling price > cost price, profit = ₹4000 - ₹3500 = ₹500. The farmer made a profit of ₹500.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why should a seller consider total cost price and not just the purchase price while determining profit or loss?
questions.answer: A seller must consider total cost price because it includes all expenses like transportation, wages, and taxes, not just the purchase price. Ignoring these expenses would give an incorrect profit or loss figure, leading to wrong business decisions.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is profit considered a sign of a successful transaction?
questions.answer: Profit indicates that the seller has earned more than what was spent, showing effective management and demand for the product. It encourages reinvestment and growth in business.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why should spoiled or damaged goods be excluded from the quantity sold?
questions.answer: Spoiled or damaged goods cannot be sold, so they represent a direct loss. Including them in sold quantity would overstate revenue and understate actual loss.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is advertising considered an expense that affects profit?
questions.answer: Advertising increases the cost of selling goods and is part of other expenses. Though it may boost sales, it must be subtracted from revenue to determine actual profit.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the process of determining profit or loss in a school fair activity like selling handicrafts. Include the steps of calculating total cost price, total selling price, and comparing them.
questions.answer: First, list all expenses: cost of materials, transportation, packaging, and any other costs. Add them to get total cost price. Then, calculate total selling price by multiplying number of items sold by selling price per item. Compare the two: if selling price > cost price, there is profit; if less, there is loss. Subtract to find the amount. This helps students understand real-life business transactions.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the concept of 'no profit, no loss' with an example. Why might a charitable organization adopt this approach?
questions.answer: 'No profit, no loss' means selling price equals total cost price, so there is neither gain nor loss. For example, if total cost is ₹1000 and items are sold for ₹1000, it's a break-even. Charitable organizations use this to cover costs while serving the community, ensuring sustainability without exploiting beneficiaries.

questions.text: Explain how to convert a fraction to a percent with an example.
questions.answer: To convert a fraction to a percent, make the denominator 100 by multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same number, then write the numerator with a percent sign. For example, to convert 3/4 to percent, multiply numerator and denominator by 25: (3×25)/(4×25) = 75/100 = 75%.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is 50% equivalent to 1/2?
questions.answer: 50% means 50 per 100, which is the fraction 50/100. Simplifying 50/100 by dividing both numerator and denominator by 50 gives 1/2. Hence, 50% = 1/2.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why do we multiply by 100 to convert a decimal to a percent?
questions.answer: We multiply by 100 because percent means per hundred. Multiplying a decimal by 100 converts it to an equivalent value out of 100, which is the definition of percent.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the concept of percentage and its importance in daily life with examples.
questions.answer: Percentage is a way of expressing a number as a fraction of 100. It is denoted by the symbol %. It is used to compare quantities, calculate discounts, interest, profit, loss, and analyze data. For example, a 20% discount on a Rs. 500 item means a saving of Rs. 100. In academics, percentage scores help compare student performance. In elections, vote percentages show popularity. Thus, percentage simplifies comparisons and decision-making in real-life situations.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the steps to convert a fraction to a percent and a percent to a fraction, with one example each.
questions.answer: To convert a fraction to a percent, multiply the fraction by 100 and add the % sign. For example, 3/5 × 100 = 60%. To convert a percent to a fraction, write the percent as a fraction with denominator 100 and simplify. For example, 40% = 40/100 = 2/5 after dividing numerator and denominator by 20. These conversions are essential for solving problems involving proportions, discounts, and interest rates.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: The price of a bicycle is Rs. 2,500. If a discount of 16% is given, what is the selling price?
questions.answer: Marked price = Rs. 2,500 Discount = 16% of 2,500 = (16/100) × 2,500 = 0.16 × 2,500 = Rs. 400 Selling price = Marked price – Discount = 2,500 – 400 = Rs. 2,100 Therefore, the selling price is Rs. 2,100.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A number is increased by 25% to become 125. Find the original number.
questions.answer: Let the original number be x. After 25% increase, the number becomes x + 25% of x = x + 0.25x = 1.25x Given that 1.25x = 125 Therefore, x = 125 / 1.25 = 100 Hence, the original number is 100.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A scooter was bought for Rs. 18,000 and sold for Rs. 15,300. Find the loss percent.
questions.answer: Cost price = Rs. 18,000 Selling price = Rs. 15,300 Loss = Cost price – Selling price = 18,000 – 15,300 = Rs. 2,700 Loss percent = (Loss / Cost price) × 100 = (2,700 / 18,000) × 100 = 0.15 × 100 = 15% Therefore, the loss percent is 15%.

questions.answer: Place the compass at the vertex and draw an arc cutting both arms. From these intersection points, draw arcs of equal radius inside the angle that intersect each other. Join the vertex to this intersection point. This ray is the angle bisector.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: What is the difference between a line and a line segment?

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is a compass used to draw a circle?
questions.answer: A compass is used to draw a circle because it has two arms: one with a fixed point (the centre) and the other with a pencil that maintains a constant distance (radius) from the centre, ensuring all points on the curve are equidistant from the centre.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why are the adjacent sides of a rectangle perpendicular to each other?
questions.answer: The adjacent sides of a rectangle are perpendicular because, by definition, a rectangle is a quadrilateral with all angles equal to 90°. This property ensures that each pair of adjacent sides meets at a right angle, making them perpendicular.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why can a set square be used to draw parallel lines?
questions.answer: A set square can be used to draw parallel lines because it has straight edges and fixed angles. When one edge is aligned with a line and the square is slid without rotation, the opposite edge remains parallel to the original line.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the steps to construct a square using only a compass and ruler.
questions.answer: 1. Draw a line segment AB of the desired side length using the ruler. 2. At point A, construct a perpendicular line to AB using the compass method (arcs from A intersecting AB, then intersecting arcs above). 3. Similarly, construct a perpendicular at B to AB. 4. With compass set to length AB, mark an arc from A on the perpendicular to get point D. 5. Mark an arc from B on its perpendicular to get point C. 6. Join points C and D. 7. ABCD is the required square with all sides equal and all angles 90°.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain how to construct an angle bisector using the folding method with trace paper.
questions.answer: 1. Draw an angle on a trace paper. 2. Fold the paper such that the two arms of the angle lie exactly on top of each other, ensuring the vertex remains fixed. 3. Press the fold firmly to create a clear crease. 4. Unfold the paper. The crease formed is the angle bisector. 5. This works because folding reflects one arm onto the other, and the crease is equidistant from both arms, thus dividing the angle into two equal parts. 6. The crease line represents the set of points equidistant from the arms, which is the definition of an angle bisector.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Draw a circle of radius 3 cm. Mark its centre as O. Draw a radius OA. At point A, construct a tangent to the circle using the tools in the compass box. Explain the steps.
questions.answer: Step 1: With O as centre and radius 3 cm, draw a circle. Step 2: Mark point A on the circumference. Step 3: Join O and A. OA is the radius. Step 4: To construct a tangent at A, we need a line perpendicular to OA at A. Step 5: Place the compass at A and draw an arc cutting OA at point P (inside the circle) and extending beyond to cut the circle again at Q (so that A is between P and Q on line OA extended). Actually, better: With A as centre and any radius, draw an arc cutting OA at P and the circle at T (on the circumference). But standard method: Since tangent ⟂ radius, construct perpendicular to OA at A. Step 5: With A as centre and radius more than half of OA, draw arcs on OA extended on both sides to get points P and Q such that AP = AQ. Step 6: With P and Q as centres and radius > half of PQ, draw two arcs intersecting at point R above OA. Step 7: Join A and R. Line AR is perpendicular to OA at A. Step 8: Since OA is radius and AR ⟂ OA at A, AR is the tangent to the circle at A. Thus, the tangent at A is constructed.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Construct an angle of 120° using compass and ruler.
questions.answer: Step 1: Draw a ray OA. Step 2: With O as centre and any convenient radius, draw an arc cutting OB at point C (where OB is along OA). Step 3: With C as centre and same radius, draw an arc cutting the first arc at D. Step 4: With D as centre and same radius, draw an arc cutting the first arc at E (so that arc CD = arc DE = radius). Step 5: Now, ∠DOE = 60° (as triangle ODE is equilateral). Step 6: But we need 120°, which is the supplement. So, extend ray OD backwards to F such that O is between D and F. Actually, better: The angle between OA and OE is 120° because arc CE is twice the radius, corresponding to 120° at centre. Correct method: Step 1: Draw ray OA. Step 2: With O as centre, draw an arc cutting OA at C. Step 3: With C as centre and same radius, draw arc cutting the first arc at D. Step 4: With D as centre and same radius, draw arc cutting the first arc at E (so that ∠COE = 120° because it spans two 60° parts). Step 5: Join O and E. Ray OE is such that ∠AOE = 120°. Proof: Each 60° arc gives 60°, so two arcs give 120°.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Draw a line segment AB = 6 cm. Construct its perpendicular bisector.
questions.answer: Step 1: Draw line segment AB = 6 cm using ruler. Step 2: With A as centre and radius more than half of AB (say 4 cm), draw arcs above and below AB. Step 3: With B as centre and same radius, draw arcs above and below AB, intersecting the previous arcs at points P (above) and Q (below). Step 4: Join points P and Q with a ruler. Step 5: Line PQ intersects AB at point O. Step 6: Then PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB because: - It passes through O, the midpoint of AB (since triangles PAQ and PBQ are congruent). - It is perpendicular to AB (by construction, as P and Q are equidistant from A and B). Thus, PQ ⟂ AB and AO = OB.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Construct an angle of 90° at the initial point of a given ray.
questions.answer: Step 1: Draw ray OA. Step 2: With O as centre and any radius, draw an arc cutting OA at P. Step 3: With P as centre and same radius, draw an arc cutting the first arc at Q. Step 4: With Q as centre and same radius, draw an arc cutting the first arc at R (so that arc PQ = arc QR = radius). Step 5: With Q and R as centres and radius more than half of QR, draw two arcs intersecting at S above the arc. Step 6: Join O and S. Step 7: Then ∠AOS = 90°. Proof: By construction, ∠POQ = 60° and ∠QOR = 60°, so ∠POR = 120°. OS bisects ∠POR, so ∠POS = 60°. But wait — correction: Actually, the standard method for 90°: After step 4, we have points P, Q, R on arc with ∠POQ = ∠QOR = 60°. Then, with Q and R as centres and radius > QR/2, draw arcs intersecting at S. Join OS. Then ∠POS = 90° because OS is the bisector of angle QOR? No. Correct: The intersection S of arcs from Q and R gives ∠QOS = 30°, so ∠POS = ∠POQ + ∠QOS = 60° + 30° = 90°. Thus, ∠AOS = 90°.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Draw a circle of radius 4 cm. Draw two radii at an angle of 60°. Measure the length of the chord connecting their endpoints.
questions.answer: Step 1: Draw a circle with centre O and radius 4 cm. Step 2: Draw radius OA. Step 3: Construct ∠AOB = 60° using compass: - With O as centre and any radius, draw arc cutting OA at C. - With C as centre and same radius, draw arc cutting the first arc at D such that ∠COD = 60°. - Join OD. Then ∠AOD = 60°. Step 4: Mark point B on the circle along OD. Step 5: Join A and B. Chord AB is formed. Step 6: In triangle OAB, OA = OB = 4 cm (radii), and ∠AOB = 60°. Step 7: Since two sides and included angle are equal, and if the third side equals the others, it is equilateral. By law of cosines: AB² = OA² + OB² - 2·OA·OB·cos(60°) = 4² + 4² - 2·4·4·(1/2) = 16 + 16 - 16 = 16 ∴ AB = √16 = 4 cm. Alternatively, since ∠AOB = 60° and OA = OB, triangle OAB is isosceles with vertex angle 60°, so base angles are (180-60)/2 = 60°, hence equilateral. Thus, AB = 4 cm.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Construct a rectangle with length 5 cm and breadth 3 cm using set square and ruler.
questions.answer: Step 1: Draw a line segment AB = 5 cm (length) using ruler. Step 2: At point A, place the set square so that one edge is along AB and the right angle corner is at A. Step 3: Draw a line segment AD = 3 cm (breadth) along the other edge of the set square (perpendicular to AB). Step 4: At point B, place the set square with one edge along BA and right angle at B. Step 5: Draw a line segment BC = 3 cm (breadth) along the other edge (perpendicular to AB). Step 6: At point D, place the set square with one edge along DA and right angle at D. Step 7: Draw a line segment DC = 5 cm (parallel to AB) using the set square (by aligning and sliding). Step 8: Join point C to B and D. Step 9: Then ABCD is a rectangle with AB = DC = 5 cm, AD = BC = 3 cm, and all angles 90°.

questions.text: Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm.
questions.answer: Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 sq.cm. Therefore, the area is 30 sq.cm.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the area of a right-angled triangle equal to half the product of the two sides forming the right angle?
questions.answer: Because a right-angled triangle is exactly half of a rectangle formed by those two sides as length and breadth. The area of the rectangle is product of the sides, so the triangle's area is half of that.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain why the perimeter of a square increases when its side increases.
questions.answer: Since perimeter of a square is 4 × side, if the side increases, the product 4 × side also increases proportionally. Hence, perimeter increases with side.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why do we use square units to measure area?
questions.answer: We use square units because area measures the number of unit squares that can fit inside a surface. A square unit (like 1 sq.cm) represents the area of a square with side 1 unit, making it a consistent and standard measure.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain how the perimeter and area of a rectangle change when its length is doubled and breadth is halved.
questions.answer: Original perimeter = 2(l + b). New length = 2l, new breadth = b/2. New perimeter = 2(2l + b/2) = 4l + b. Compare: original perimeter is 2l + 2b. The new perimeter may increase or decrease depending on values. For area: original = l × b. New area = (2l) × (b/2) = l × b. So area remains the same. Thus, area stays unchanged while perimeter changes based on l and b.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe an activity to find the area of an irregular leaf using graph paper.
questions.answer: Place the leaf on graph paper and trace its outline. Count the number of complete squares inside the outline. For squares more than half inside, count them as full. Ignore squares less than half inside. Add the count of full and more-than-half squares to get approximate area in square units. This method works because each square represents a known unit area, and the total gives an estimate of the leaf's area.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: The length of a rectangle is 3 cm more than its breadth. If its perimeter is 26 cm, find its length, breadth, and area.
questions.answer: Let breadth = x cm. Then length = (x + 3) cm. Perimeter = 2(length + breadth) = 2((x + 3) + x) = 2(2x + 3) = 4x + 6. Given perimeter = 26 cm. So, 4x + 6 = 26 → 4x = 20 → x = 5. Thus, breadth = 5 cm, length = 5 + 3 = 8 cm. Area = length × breadth = 8 × 5 = 40 sq.cm. Hence, length = 8 cm, breadth = 5 cm, area = 40 sq.cm.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A square and a rectangle have equal perimeters. If the side of the square is 10 cm and the length of the rectangle is 14 cm, find the breadth of the rectangle and compare their areas.
questions.answer: Perimeter of square = 4 × side = 4 × 10 = 40 cm. Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth) = 2(14 + b) = 28 + 2b. Set equal: 28 + 2b = 40 → 2b = 12 → b = 6 cm. Area of square = side² = 10 × 10 = 100 sq.cm. Area of rectangle = length × breadth = 14 × 6 = 84 sq.cm. Thus, breadth of rectangle is 6 cm, and the square has greater area (100 > 84).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: The area of a rectangular plot is 120 sq.m and its length is 15 m. Find its perimeter.
questions.answer: Area = length × breadth → 120 = 15 × b → b = 120 ÷ 15 = 8 m. Perimeter = 2(length + breadth) = 2(15 + 8) = 2 × 23 = 46 m. Hence, the perimeter is 46 m.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A floor is 6 m long and 4.5 m wide. It is to be covered with square tiles of side 30 cm. How many tiles are required?
questions.answer: Convert tile side to metres: 30 cm = 0.3 m. Area of floor = 6 × 4.5 = 27 sq.m. Area of one tile = 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09 sq.m. Number of tiles = Area of floor ÷ Area of one tile = 27 ÷ 0.09 = 300. Hence, 300 tiles are required.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A garden in the shape of a right triangle has two perpendicular sides measuring 8 m and 6 m. Find the area of the garden and the length of the fence needed to surround it (perimeter).
questions.answer: Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 8 × 6 = 24 sq.m. To find perimeter, we need the hypotenuse. By Pythagoras: hypotenuse = √(8² + 6²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 m. Perimeter = 8 + 6 + 10 = 24 m. Hence, area = 24 sq.m and perimeter = 24 m.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: The perimeter of a regular hexagon is 48 cm. Find the length of each side and its perimeter if each side is increased by 2 cm.
questions.answer: Perimeter of regular hexagon = 6 × side. So, 6 × side = 48 → side = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm. If each side is increased by 2 cm, new side = 8 + 2 = 10 cm. New perimeter = 6 × 10 = 60 cm. Hence, original side = 8 cm, new perimeter = 60 cm.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A rectangular field is 50 m long and 30 m wide. A path of 2 m width is built inside around the field. Find the area of the path.
questions.answer: Area of outer field = 50 × 30 = 1500 sq.m. Inner dimensions after path: length = 50 - 2×2 = 46 m, breadth = 30 - 2×2 = 26 m. Area of inner field = 46 × 26 = 1196 sq.m. Area of path = outer area - inner area = 1500 - 1196 = 304 sq.m. Hence, the area of the path is 304 sq.m.

questions.text: Explain how you would verify the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem using square pieces of paper.
questions.answer: Cut square pieces of paper of unit side. Arrange them to form squares on the two shorter sides of a right angled triangle and count the total number of pieces. Then arrange the same pieces to form a square on the hypotenuse. If the number of pieces used in both cases is equal, the theorem is verified.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: What is a Pythagorean triplet? Give two examples.
questions.answer: A Pythagorean triplet is a set of three natural numbers such that the square of the largest number equals the sum of the squares of the other two. Examples: (3, 4, 5) and (5, 12, 13).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the hypotenuse always the longest side in a right angled triangle?
questions.answer: Because the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, which is greater than the square of either side alone. Hence, the hypotenuse must be longer than each of the other sides.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: How can you check if a triangle with sides 7 cm, 24 cm, and 25 cm is right angled?
questions.answer: Calculate the squares: 7² = 49, 24² = 576, 25² = 625. Since 49 + 576 = 625, the condition of the theorem is satisfied. Therefore, the triangle is right angled.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the triangle with sides 11 cm, 60 cm, and 61 cm a right angled triangle?
questions.answer: Because 11² + 60² = 121 + 3600 = 3721, and 61² = 3721. Since the sum of the squares of the two smaller sides equals the square of the largest side, the triangle satisfies the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem and is therefore right angled.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain why (9, 40, 41) is a Baudhayana-Pythagorean triplet.
questions.answer: Because 9² = 81, 40² = 1600, and 81 + 1600 = 1681, which equals 41² = 1681. Hence, the set (9, 40, 41) satisfies the condition of the theorem and is a Baudhayana-Pythagorean triplet.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the triangle with sides 10 cm, 24 cm, and 26 cm right angled?
questions.answer: Because 10² + 24² = 100 + 576 = 676, and 26² = 676. Since the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides equals the square of the longest side, the triangle is right angled by the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the activity to verify the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem using square pieces of paper or cardboard.
questions.answer: Cut several square pieces of paper or cardboard, each of side one unit. Take a right angled triangle and measure the lengths of the two sides forming the right angle and the hypotenuse. Place the square pieces to form a square on each side. Count the number of pieces used in the square on each side. You will find that the number of pieces in the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the pieces in the squares on the other two sides. This verifies that the area of the square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides, thus confirming the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem with its historical background and give two examples of its application in daily life.
questions.answer: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem states that in a right angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. It was discovered by the Indian mathematician Baudhayana in the 8th century BC, later attributed to Pythagoras. In daily life, it is used in construction to ensure walls are perpendicular by checking diagonals. It is also used in navigation to find the shortest distance between two points, and in laying out rectangular fields or gardens by verifying right angles using the 3-4-5 rule.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A ladder 17 m long is placed against a wall such that its foot is 8 m from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
questions.answer: Let the height reached be h m. The ladder, wall, and ground form a right angled triangle with hypotenuse = 17 m and base = 8 m. By Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem: (hypotenuse)² = (base)² + (height)² (17)² = (8)² + h² 289 = 64 + h² h² = 289 - 64 = 225 h = √225 = 15 m Hence, the ladder reaches 15 m up the wall.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Find the length of the diagonal of a rectangle with sides 9 cm and 12 cm.
questions.answer: The diagonal of a rectangle divides it into two right angled triangles. In each triangle, the sides are 9 cm and 12 cm, and the diagonal is the hypotenuse. Let the diagonal be d cm. By Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem: d² = 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225 d = √225 = 15 cm Hence, the length of the diagonal is 15 cm.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A person walks 15 m west and then 20 m north. How far is he from the starting point?
questions.answer: The path forms a right angled triangle with legs 15 m and 20 m. The distance from the starting point is the hypotenuse. Let the distance be d m. d² = 15² + 20² = 225 + 400 = 625 d = √625 = 25 m Hence, the person is 25 m from the starting point.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: The sides of a triangle are 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm. Verify if it is a right angled triangle.
questions.answer: The longest side is 10 cm. Square of longest side = 10² = 100 Sum of squares of other two sides = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 Since 100 = 100, the condition of Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem is satisfied. Hence, the triangle is right angled.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Find the length of the unknown side in a right angled triangle if the hypotenuse is 25 cm and one side is 7 cm.
questions.answer: Let the unknown side be x cm. By Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem: (hypotenuse)² = (side1)² + (side2)² 25² = 7² + x² 625 = 49 + x² x² = 625 - 49 = 576 x = √576 = 24 cm Hence, the unknown side is 24 cm.

questions.text: A door is 2 m wide and 2.1 m high. Is the diagonal of the door longer than 3 m?
questions.answer: Let the diagonal be d m. d² = 2² + 2.1² = 4 + 4.41 = 8.41 d = √8.41 ≈ 2.9 m Since 2.9 m < 3 m, the diagonal is not longer than 3 m.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the concept of simple interest with the formula and solve one example.
questions.answer: Simple interest is the interest calculated uniformly on the original principal for the entire loan or deposit period. The formula is: Simple Interest = (Principal × Rate × Time) / 100. For example, if Rs 4000 is deposited at 5 p.c.p.a. for 1 year, interest = (4000 × 5 × 1) / 100 = Rs 200. Therefore, the amount after one year is Principal + Interest = 4000 + 200 = Rs 4200.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: Shrushti keeps Rs 35,000 in a bank at the rate of 8% per annum. How much interest will she get in one year? Also, find the amount she will have after one year.
questions.answer: Principal = Rs 35,000 Rate of interest = 8% p.a. Time = 1 year Simple Interest = (Principal × Rate × Time) / 100 = (35000 × 8 × 1) / 100 = 280000 / 100 = Rs 2,800 Amount = Principal + Interest = 35000 + 2800 = Rs 37,800 Therefore, interest earned = Rs 2,800 and total amount after one year = Rs 37,800.

questions.answer: Principal = Rs 1,30,000 Rate = 11% p.a. Time = 1 year Interest = (130000 × 11 × 1) / 100 = 1430000 / 100 = Rs 14,300 Amount = Principal + Interest = 130000 + 14300 = Rs 1,44,300 Therefore, interest to be paid = Rs 14,300 and total amount to be repaid = Rs 1,44,300.

questions.text: How is a frequency table constructed from raw data?
questions.answer: First, list all the unique scores in ascending order in the first column. Then, for each score, draw tally marks for each occurrence, grouping them in sets of five. Finally, count the tally marks and write the total in the frequency column.

questions.text: Explain the steps to draw a bar graph.
questions.answer: First, draw the X-axis and Y-axis. Then, choose a suitable scale for the Y-axis based on the data. Label the X-axis with the categories and the Y-axis with the scale. Draw bars for each category with heights proportional to their values, keeping the width of all bars uniform.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: What are the characteristics of a bar graph?
questions.answer: In a bar graph, data is represented by vertical or horizontal rectangular columns of equal width. The height of each column corresponds to the frequency of the item it represents. Bar graphs make it easy to compare different items visually.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: How are infographics useful in presenting information?
questions.answer: Infographics present information in an artistic and attractive way using images, diagrams, and colours. They make complex data easy to understand and remember, and help in quick interpretation.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why are scores written in ascending order in a frequency table?
questions.answer: Scores are written in ascending order to make the table organized and easy to read. It helps in quickly locating a particular score and comparing frequencies. This order also aids in calculating measures like median later.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is a bar graph better than a pictograph for showing data like 24 books read by Sushil?
questions.answer: A pictograph may not accurately show small numbers like 24 if the symbol represents a large value. A bar graph allows precise representation using a scale, so even small values can be shown accurately by adjusting the height of the bar.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the width of bars kept uniform in a bar graph?
questions.answer: The width is kept uniform so that only the height of the bars varies, which represents the data. If widths varied, it would be difficult to compare the heights accurately and could mislead the viewer.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the importance of data representation in daily life with examples.
questions.answer: Data representation helps us understand information quickly and clearly. For example, a bar graph showing monthly expenses helps a family see where they spend the most. A frequency table of test scores helps a teacher see how many students passed or failed. Infographics in newspapers show weather or sports data in an attractive way. In schools, pictographs help young students understand numbers through pictures. In hospitals, bar graphs show patient recovery trends. Thus, representing data visually saves time, reduces errors, and helps in making better decisions.

questions.answer: Ramanujan's square is formed by arranging the numbers from his date of birth (22-12-1887) in a 4x4 grid such that the sum of each row, column and diagonal is the same. questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the process to find the lighter object among 9 identical objects using a pan balance in minimum steps.
questions.answer: First, divide the 9 objects into three groups of three. Weigh two groups against each other. If they balance, the lighter object is in the third group; otherwise, it is in the lighter group. Then take the group with the lighter object, weigh two of them. If they balance, the third is lighter; otherwise, the lighter one on the scale is the answer. This uses the pan balance only twice.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain why the new square formed in the activity has an area equal to the sum of the areas of the two original squares.
questions.answer: When the two squares are cut and rearranged as shown, the total area remains unchanged because no material is added or removed. The pieces are reconfigured to form a single square, so its area must equal the combined area of the two original squares. This demonstrates the geometric proof of the Pythagorean theorem for squares.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: What observations can be made from the Tower of Hanoi move table as the number of discs increases?
questions.answer: As the number of discs increases by one, the minimum number of moves approximately doubles and then increases by one. The pattern follows the formula 2^n - 1, showing exponential growth. For example, 3 discs take 7 moves, 4 discs take 15, 5 discs take 31, and so on.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is a larger disc not allowed to be placed on a smaller disc in Tower of Hanoi?
questions.answer: This rule ensures the game follows a logical sequence and prevents invalid configurations. If larger discs could be placed on smaller ones, the goal of maintaining order would be lost, and the puzzle could be trivially solved or become unsolvable in the intended way. The rule maintains the challenge and mathematical integrity of the problem.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why does the pan balance method work to find the lighter object in minimum steps?
questions.answer: The pan balance divides the search space into three parts with each weighing, making it efficient. Each outcome (left heavy, right heavy, or equal) gives maximum information, reducing the possibilities to one-third. This ternary search strategy minimizes the number of weighings needed, which is why 2 weighings suffice for 9 objects.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Why is the sum the same in all rows, columns and diagonals of Ramanujan's square?
questions.answer: The numbers are arranged using mathematical patterns and properties of magic squares, where specific positions ensure equal sums. Ramanujan's square is a special case of a 4x4 magic square constructed using his birth date, designed so that all lines sum to 139 through careful placement and number relationships.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Describe the Tower of Hanoi game, its rules, and how to solve it for 3 discs. Include the pattern of moves and the formula for minimum moves.
questions.answer: The Tower of Hanoi is a mathematical puzzle consisting of three rods and a number of discs of different sizes that can slide onto any rod. The puzzle starts with the discs stacked in ascending order of size on one rod, the smallest at the top. The objective is to move the entire stack to another rod, obeying the rules: only one disc can be moved at a time, and a larger disc cannot be placed on top of a smaller disc. For 3 discs, the minimum number of moves is 7. The sequence involves moving the top two discs to the auxiliary rod, then the largest to the target rod, and finally the two discs onto the largest. The general formula for n discs is 2^n - 1 moves, showing exponential growth. This puzzle teaches recursion and problem-solving strategies.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: Explain the activity of forming a new square from two squares (one with side half the other) as described in the chapter. What does it demonstrate about areas?
questions.answer: The activity involves cutting out a square of side 6 units and another of side 3 units (half of 6). The smaller square is glued to the larger one, and lines are drawn from the midpoint of the side of the large square to the opposite vertices. After cutting along these lines and rearranging the pieces, a new square is formed. This new square has an area equal to the sum of the areas of the two original squares (36 + 9 = 45 sq units), demonstrating that the area of the new square is the sum. This activity visually proves that when figures are rearranged without overlap or gap, the total area remains conserved. It also relates to the Pythagorean theorem, as the sides 3 and 6 can be thought of as legs, and the new square's side as hypotenuse in a right triangle context, though here it's purely additive. The key learning is that area is additive under dissection and rearrangement.

questions.answer: The formula for minimum moves in Tower of Hanoi is 2^n - 1, where n is the number of discs. For n = 5: 2^5 = 32 32 - 1 = 31 Therefore, the minimum number of moves required is 31.

questions.text: A square has a side of 4 units. Another square has a side of 6 units. If they are rearranged as per the activity to form a new square, what is the area of the new square?
questions.answer: Area of first square = side^2 = 4^2 = 16 sq units Area of second square = side^2 = 6^2 = 36 sq units Total area = 16 + 36 = 52 sq units Since the new square is formed by rearranging the two squares without loss or overlap, its area equals the sum of the areas. Hence, area of new square = 52 sq units.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: त्रिकोणी चिती व इष्टिकाचितीतील पृष्ठे व शिरोबिंदूंची संख्या तुलना करा.
questions.answer: त्रिकोणी चितीतील 6 शिरोबिंदू, 3 आयताकृती पृष्ठे, 2 त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे असतात. इष्टिकाचितीतील 8 शिरोबिंदू, 6 आयताकृती पृष्ठे असतात. त्रिकोणी चितीमध्ये शिरोबिंदू कमी व पृष्ठे वेगळे असतात.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: वृत्तचिती व शंकूतील पृष्ठे तुलना करा.
questions.answer: वृत्तचितीतील 2 वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठ व 1 वक्र पृष्ठ असतात. शंकूतील 1 वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठ व 1 वक्र पृष्ठ असतो. वृत्तचितीमध्ये दोन सपाट पृष्ठ असतात, तर शंकूमध्ये फक्त एक.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: त्रिकोणी सूची व चौकोनी सूचीतील शिरोबिंदू व कडांची संख्या लिहा.
questions.answer: त्रिकोणी सूचीतील 4 शिरोबिंदू व 6 कडा असतात. चौकोनी सूचीतील 5 शिरोबिंदू व 8 कडा असतात.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: घन व इष्टिकाचितीतील पृष्ठे तुलना करा.
questions.answer: घन व इष्टिकाचिती दोन्हींची पृष्ठे आयताकृती असतात. घनतील सर्व पृष्ठे चौरस असतात, तर इष्टिकाचितीमध्ये पृष्ठे आयताकृती असतात ज्यांची लांबी व रुंदी वेगळी असू शकते.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: वृत्तचितीला शिरोबिंदू कदाचित नसते का?
questions.answer: वृत्तचितीतील पृष्ठे वक्र असतात, त्यामुळे कडे व शिरोबिंदू निर्माण होत नाही. वक्र पृष्ठात कोणे नसते, त्यामुळे शिरोबिंदू नाही.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: शंकूला कडा नसते का?
questions.answer: शंकूची आधार वर्तुळाकृती असली व वक्र पृष्ठ आधाराशी एकत्र येतो, त्यामुळे कोणे निर्माण होत नाही. कडा हा दोन सपाट पृष्ठांचा सामाईक असतो, त्यामुळे शंकूला कडा नाही.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: घन ही इष्टिकाचिती कशी?
questions.answer: घन हे सर्व पृष्ठे समान आकारचे असलेली इष्टिकाचिती असते. घनतील सर्व पृष्ठे चौरस असतात, ज्यामुळे ते इष्टिकाचितीचा एक विशिष्ट प्रकार होतो.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: त्रिकोणी चिती, इष्टिकाचिती, वृत्तचिती व शंकू यांचे घटक तुलना करा व त्यांचे नावे, शिरोबिंदू, पृष्ठे, कडा लिहा.
questions.answer: त्रिकोणी चिती: 6 शिरोबिंदू, 2 त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे, 3 आयताकृती पृष्ठे, 9 कडा. इष्टिकाचिती: 8 शिरोबिंदू, 6 आयताकृती पृष्ठे, 12 कडा. वृत्तचिती: 0 शिरोबिंदू, 2 वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे, 1 वक्र पृष्ठ, 1 वर्तुळाकार कडा. शंकू: 1 शिरोबिंदू, 1 वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठ, 1 वक्र पृष्ठ, 0 कडा. त्रिकोणी चिती व इष्टिकाचितीमध्ये सपाट पृष्ठे असतात, तर वृत्तचिती व शंकूमध्ये वक्र पृष्ठ असतात. शिरोबिंदू व कडा फक्त सपाट पृष्ठांच्या आकारांमध्ये निर्माण होतात.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: त्रिमितीय आकारांचे प्रकार लिहा व त्यांचे उदाहरण द्या. त्यांचे घटक (शिरोबिंदू, पृष्ठे, कडा) आधारावर तुलना करा.
questions.answer: त्रिमितीय आकारांचे प्रमुख प्रकार: चिती (त्रिकोणी, इष्टिकाचिती, बहुभुजी), सूची (त्रिकोणी, चौकोनी, बहुभुजी), वृत्तचिती (दंडगोल), शंकू. चिती व सूचीमध्ये शिरोबिंदू, सपाट पृष्ठे, कडा असतात. वृत्तचितीमध्ये वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे, वक्र पृष्ठे, वर्तुळाकार कडा असतात, शिरोबिंदू नाही. शंकूमध्ये शिरोबिंदू, वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठ, वक्र पृष्ठ असतात, कडा नाही. त्रिकोणी चिती: 6 शिरोबिंदू, 5 पृष्ठे (2 त्रिकोणी + 3 आयताकृती), 9 कडा. इष्टिकाचिती: 8 शिरोबिंदू, 6 पृष्ठे, 12 कडा. त्रिकोणी सूची: 4 शिरोबिंदू, 4 पृष्ठे, 6 कडा. चौकोनी सूची: 5 शिरोबिंदू, 5 पृष्ठे (4 त्रिकोणी + 1 चौरस), 8 कडा. वृत्तचिती: 0 शिरोबिंदू, 3 पृष्ठे (2 वर्तुळाकृती + 1 वक्र), 1 कडा. शंकू: 1 शिरोबिंदू, 2 पृष्ठे (1 वर्तुळाकृती + 1 वक्र), 0 कडा.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरण सोडवा व पूर्ण कार्य द्या.
questions.text: त्रिकोणी चिती तयार करण्यासाठी 12 त्रिकोण वापरले. त्यामुळे तयार झालेल्या त्रिकोणी चितीतील शिरोबिंदू, पृष्ठे, कडांची संख्या कiti?
questions.answer: त्रिकोणी चिती तयार करण्यासाठी वापरले जाणारे त्रिकोण = 12 त्रिकोणी चितीला 2 त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे व 3 आयताकृती पृष्ठे मिळतात. एक त्रिकोणी चितीसाठी 2 त्रिकोण व 3 आयताकृती पृष्ठे लागतात. 12 त्रिकोण वापरली तर त्रिकोणी चितींची संख्या = 12 / 2 = 6 एक त्रिकोणी चितीसाठी: - शिरोबिंदू = 6 - त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे = 2 - आयताकृती पृष्ठे = 3 - कडा = 9 6 त्रिकोणी चितींसाठी: - एकूण शिरोबिंदू = 6 × 6 = 36 - एकूण त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे = 6 × 2 = 12 - एकूण आयताकृती पृष्ठे = 6 × 3 = 18 - एकूण कडा = 6 × 9 = 54 उत्तर: शिरोबिंदू = 36, पृष्ठे = 12 त्रिकोणी + 18 आयताकृती = 30, कडा = 54

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरण सोडवा व पूर्ण कार्य द्या.
questions.text: इष्टिकाचिती तयार करण्यासाठी 18 आयत वापरले. त्यामुळे तयार झालेल्या इष्टिकाचितीतील शिरोबिंदू, पृष्ठे, कडांची संख्या कiti?
questions.answer: इष्टिकाचिती तयार करण्यासाठी वापरले जाणारे आयत = 18 इष्टिकाचितीला 6 आयताकृती पृष्ठे मिळतात. एक इष्टिकाचितीसाठी 6 आयत लागतात. 18 आयत वापरली तर इष्टिकाचितीची संख्या = 18 / 6 = 3 एक इष्टिकाचितीसाठी: - शिरोबिंदू = 8 - आयताकृती पृष्ठे = 6 - कडा = 12 3 इष्टिकाचितींसाठी: - एकूण शिरोबिंदू = 3 × 8 = 24 - एकूण आयताकृती पृष्ठे = 3 × 6 = 18 - एकूण कडा = 3 × 12 = 36 उत्तर: शिरोबिंदू = 24, पृष्ठे = 18, कडा = 36

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरण सोडवा व पूर्ण कार्य द्या.
questions.text: वृत्तचिती (दंडगोल) तयार करण्यासाठी 10 वर्तुळे वापरले. त्यामुळे तयार झालेल्या वृत्तचितीतील वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे, वक्र पृष्ठे, वर्तुळाकार कडांची संख्या कiti?
questions.answer: वृत्तचिती तयार करण्यासाठी वापरले जाणारे वर्तुळ = 10 वृत्तचितीला 2 वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे व 1 वक्र पृष्ठ मिळतात. एक वृत्तचितीसाठी 2 वर्तुळ व 1 वक्र पृष्ठ लागतात. 10 वर्तुळ वापरली तर वृत्तचितीची संख्या = 10 / 2 = 5 एक वृत्तचितीसाठी: - वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे = 2 - वक्र पृष्ठे = 1 - वर्तुळाकार कडा = 1 5 वृत्तचितींसाठी: - एकूण वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे = 5 × 2 = 10 - एकूण वक्र पृष्ठे = 5 × 1 = 5 - एकूण वर्तुळाकार कडा = 5 × 1 = 5 उत्तर: वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे = 10, वक्र पृष्ठे = 5, वर्तुळाकार कडा = 5

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरण सोडवा व पूर्ण कार्य द्या.
questions.text: शंकू तयार करण्यासाठी 5 वर्तुळे व 5 त्रिकोण वापरले. त्यामुळे तयार झालेल्या शंकूतील शिरोबिंदू, वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे, वक्र पृष्ठे कiti?
questions.answer: शंकू तयार करण्यासाठी: - आधार: 1 वर्तुळ - वक्र पृष्ठ: त्रिकोणे जुळून (प्रति शंकूसाठी 1 त्रिकोण) 5 वर्तुळ वापरली तर शंकूंची संख्या = 5 / 1 = 5 (आधारासाठी) 5 त्रिकोण वापरली तर शंकूंची संख्या = 5 / 1 = 5 (वक्र पृष्ठासाठी) शंकूंची संख्या = 5 एक शंकूसाठी: - शिरोबिंदू = 1 - वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे = 1 - वक्र पृष्ठे = 1 5 शंकूंसाठी: - एकूण शिरोबिंदू = 5 × 1 = 5 - एकूण वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे = 5 × 1 = 5 - एकूण वक्र पृष्ठे = 5 × 1 = 5 उत्तर: शिरोबिंदू = 5, वर्तुळाकृती पृष्ठे = 5, वक्र पृष्ठे = 5

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरण सोडवा व पूर्ण कार्य द्या.
questions.text: त्रिकोणी सूची तयार करण्यासाठी 8 त्रिकोण वापरले. त्यामुळे तयार झालेल्या त्रिकोणी सूचीतील शिरोबिंदू, पृष्ठे, कडांची संख्या कiti?
questions.answer: त्रिकोणी सूची तयार करण्यासाठी वापरले जाणारे त्रिकोण = 8 त्रिकोणी सूचीला 4 त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे मिळतात. एक त्रिकोणी सूचिसाठी 4 त्रिकोण लागतात. 8 त्रिकोण वापरली तर त्रिकोणी सूचींची संख्या = 8 / 4 = 2 एक त्रिकोणी सूचिसाठी: - शिरोबिंदू = 4 - त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे = 4 - कडा = 6 2 त्रिकोणी सूचींसाठी: - एकूण शिरोबिंदू = 2 × 4 = 8 - एकूण त्रिकोणी पृष्ठे = 2 × 4 = 8 - एकूण कडा = 2 × 6 = 12 उत्तर: शिरोबिंदू = 8, पृष्ठे = 8, कडा = 12

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरण सोडवा व पूर्ण कार्य द्या.
questions.text: चौकोनी सूची तयार करण्यासाठी 4 चौरस व 4 त्रिकोण वापरले. त्यामुळे तयार झालेल्या चौकोनी सूचीतील शिरोबिंदू, पृष्ठे, कडांची संख्या कiti?
questions.answer: चौकोनी सूची तयार करण्यासाठी: - तळाचा पृष्ठ: 1 चौरस - उभी पृष्ठे: 4 त्रिकोण एक चौकोनी सूचिसाठी 1 चौरस व 4 त्रिकोण लागतात. 4 चौरस वापरली तर चौकोनी सूचींची संख्या = 4 / 1 = 4 4 त्रिकोण वापरली तर चौकोनी सूचींची संख्या = 4 / 4 = 1 शंकितता: त्रिकोण सीमित आहे, त्यामुही 1 सूची तयार होईल. एक चौकोनी सूचिसाठी: - शिरोबिंदू = 5 - पृष्ठे = 5 (1 चौरस + 4 त्रिकोण) - कडा = 8 1 चौकोनी सूचिसाठी: - शिरोबिंदू = 5 - पृष्ठे = 5 - कडा = 8 उत्तर: शिरोबिंदू = 5, पृष्ठे = 5, कडा = 8

questions.text: घड्याळात 9 वाजले असताना तास काटा व मिनिट काटा यांच्यामध्ये कोणते कोन तयार होतो? त्याचा प्रकार काय आहे?
questions.answer: तास काटा 9 वाजला आहे, त्यामुळे 9 * 30° = 270°. मिनिट काटा 12 वाजला आहे, त्यामुळे 0°. त्यामुळे कोनाचा माप = |270° - 0°| = 270°. 270° 180° पेक्षा मोठा व 360° पेक्षा लहान असल्यामुळे तो प्रविशालकोन आहे.

questions.answer: 45° असलेला कोन लघुकोन आहे (0° पेक्षा मोठा व 90° पेक्षा लहान). दुप्पट केल्याने 45° * 2 = 90°. 90° असलेला कोन काटकोन आहे.

questions.text: नैसर्गिक संख्या, पूर्ण संख्या व पूर्णांक संख्या यांचे संक्षिप्त माहिती द्या.
questions.answer: नैसर्गिक संख्या म्हणजे 1, 2, 3, ... असे गणतोय, जी मोजण्यासाठी वापरली जाते. पूर्ण संख्या म्हणजे 0, 1, 2, 3, ... असे गणतोय, जी नैसर्गिक संख्या समूहात शून्य जोड केल्याने तयार होते. पूर्णांक संख्या म्हणजे शून्य, सर्व धन संख्या (1, 2, 3, ...) व सर्व क्रण संख्या (-1, -2, -3, ...) यांचा संयोजन. नैसर्गिक संख्या शून्य समाविष्ट न करते, तर पूर्ण संख्या शून्य समाविष्ट करते. पूर्णांक संख्या धन व क्रण संख्यांचा समावेश करते, ज्यामुळे ते सर्वात विस्तृत संख्या समूह आहे.

questions.answer: सममूल्य अपूर्णांक म्हणजे वेगवेगळे अंक लिहिल्याप्रमाणे पण मूल्य समान असलेले अपूर्णांक.

questions.instruction: खालील प्रश्नांची एक वाक्यात उत्तरे लिहा.

questions.answer: अंशाधिक अपूर्णांक म्हणजे अंश छेदापेक्षा मोठा असलेला अपूर्णांक.

questions.answer: पूर्णांकयुक्त अपूर्णांक म्हणजे एक पूर्णांक व एक अपूर्णांकचे संयोजन.
