questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: चालू खाते व बचत खात्यांचे दोन फरक सांगा.
questions.answer: चालू खाते मुख्यतः व्यापारींकरिता असतात व त्यावर व्याज दिला जात नाही. बचत खाते व्यक्तिगत बचतकरिता असतात व त्यावर दररोजच्या शिल्लकवर व्याज दिला जातो. चालू खात्यामध्ये अपेक्षित सीमा बिना कितीही वेळा पैसे काढता येईल, तर बचत खात्यामध्ये काढण्यावर पाबंदी असते.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: बँक पासबुकातील शिल्लक कसे काढते?
questions.answer: बँक पासबुकातील शिल्लक जमा रक्कम व काढली गeli रक्कमचा फरक असतो. प्रत्येक नोंदनंतर जमा जोडलेली व काढली गeli रक्कम घटली जाते. अंतिम शिल्लक खात्यातील उपलब्ध रक्कम दर्शवते.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: सरळव्याज सूत्र व्युत्पन्न करा.
questions.answer: सरळव्याज सूत्र म्हणजे I = P × R × T / 100. येथे I = व्याज, P = मुद्दल, R = वार्षिक दर (शे.), T = मुदत (वर्षे). 100 रुपये मुद्दलावर R रुपये व्याज असल्यास, P रुपये मुद्दलावर 1 वर्षाचे व्याज P × R / 100 असते. T वर्षांसाठी ते T वाढवले जाते, त्यामुळे I = P × R × T / 100.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: आवर्ती ठेव खाते व मुदत ठेवींचे फरक सांगा.
questions.answer: आवर्ती ठेव खात्यामध्ये प्रत्येक महिन्याला ठराविक रक्कम जमा केली जाते, ज्यामुळे बचत वाढते. मुदत ठेव खात्यामध्ये एकाच वेळी ठराविक रक्कम ठरावीक कालावधीसाठी जमा केली जाते. आवर्ती ठेववरील व्याज दर मुदत ठेवापेक्षा कमी असतो, तर मुदत ठेववरील व्याज दर जास्त असतो.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: बँक चालू खातेवर व्याज देत नाही का?
questions.answer: बँक चालू खातेवर व्याज देत नाही कारण यामध्ये ठेवी खूप अस्थिर असतात. खातेदार एका दिवसात कितीही वेळा पैसे जमा करतो व काढतो, त्यामुळे बँक त्याची रक्कम स्थिरपणे वापरू शकत नाही. व्याज देण्यासाठी बँकला लांब कालावधीसाठी ठेवीची गरज असते, जे चालू खात्यामध्ये उपलब्ध नाहीत. त्यामुळे चालू खातेवर व्याज दिला जात नाही.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: मुदत ठेवीवरील व्याज दर बचत खातेपेक्षा जास्त का?
questions.answer: मुदत ठेवीवरील व्याज दर जास्त असतो कारण बँकला लांब कालावधीसाठी ठेवी मिळते, ज्यामुथे ती रक्कम लाभदायक धंध्यांमध्ये गुंतवू शकते. बचत खात्यामध्ये ठेवी अल्पकालीन असती व अचानक काढली जाऊ शकते, त्यामुळे बँक जोखिम घेतली. त्यामुळे बचत खातेवर व्याज दर कमी ठेवला जातो, तर मुदत ठेवीवर जास्त.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: बँक पासबुक शेयर करणे जोखिमदायक का?
questions.answer: बँक पासबुक शेयर करणे जोखिमदायक असतो कारण त्यात खात्याचे संपूर्ण विवरण जसे की खाते क्रमांक, शिल्लक, जमा व काढली गeli रक्कमची नोंद असते. जर हा माहिती अनधिकारी हातांमध्ये पडली तर खात्याचा दुरुपयोग होऊ शके, जसे की नकली चेक लिहिणे किंवा अनधिकारी काढणे. त्यामुळे पासबुक गोपनीय ठेवणे आवश्यक आहे.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: बँक पासबुकाचे महत्त्व व त्यात दर्शवितलेली माहिती सांगा.
questions.answer: बँक पासबुक खात्याचे वैयक्तिक रेकॉर्ड असतो, ज्यासाठी खात्याचे सर्व लेन-देन नोंदले जाते. त्यात तारीख, तपशील (जमा/काढ/व्याज), रक्कम, व शिल्लक दर्शवितले होते. पासबुक दर्शवते की खात्याची शेवटची स्थिति काय आहे, ज्यामुळे खात्याचे आर्थिक व्यवस्थापन सोपे होतो. ते बँकेसाठी प्रमाणपत्र म्हणून कार्य करते, जसे की लोन अर्जन्यासाठी. पासबुकातील नोंदींचे तपास करून खात्याचे अचूकता यापरता येईल. त्यामुळे पासबुक वित्तीय पारदर्शकता व जबाबदारी वाढवते.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: सरळव्याजाची गणना करण्याचे पद्धती व त्याचे वापर सांगा.
questions.answer: सरळव्याजाची गणना सूत्र I = P × R × T / 100 वापरून केली जाते, जेथे P = मुद्दल, R = वार्षिक व्याज दर (शे.), T = मुदत (वर्षे). पहिल्यांदाच एक वर्षाचा व्याज P × R / 100 काढला जातो, त्यानंतर ते T वा गुणले जाते. उदाहरणार्थ, 5000 रुपये मुद्दलावर 6% दराने 2 वर्षे व्याज = 5000 × 6 × 2 / 100 = 600 रुपये. रास = मुद्दल + व्याज. सरळव्याजेचा वापर बचत खाते, ठेवी, कर्ज व शिक्षण योजनांमध्ये होतो. ते सोपे व स्पष्ट असल्यामुळे विद्यार्थ्यांना समजणे सोपे.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील प्रश्नांचे उत्तर द्या व पूर्ण कामकाज दाखवा.
questions.text: शाळेची संचयिकेने 10000 रुपये 5% वार्षिक दराने 1 वर्षांसाठी ठेवी केली. प्रत्येक महिन्याने किती व्याज मिळतो?
questions.answer: मुद्दल (P) = 10000 रुपये व्याज दर (R) = 5% वार्षिक मुदत (T) = 1 वर्ष वर्षभर व्याज (I) = P × R × T / 100 I = 10000 × 5 × 1 / 100 I = 50000 / 100 I = 500 रुपये महिनेवारी व्याज = 500 / 12 ≈ 41.67 रुपये उत्तर: प्रत्येक महिन्याने लगभग 41.67 रुपये व्याज मिळतो.

questions.text: त्रिज्या दुगुण केल्यास परीघ देखील दुगुण होतो का?
questions.answer: होय, कारण परीघ = 2πr. त्रिज्या र दुगुण केल्यास परीघ देखील दुगुण होतो, कारण 2π (2r) = 2 × (2πr). हे रैखिक संबंध दर्शवतो.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: वर्तुळाच्या परीघ, व्यास, त्रिज्या व π यांचे संबंध स्पष्ट करा. उधा उदाहरणे द्या.
questions.answer: वर्तुळाच्या परीघ (C) व त्याच्या व्यास (d)चे गुणोत्तर π (पाय) असतो, ज्यामध्ये C = πd. त्रिज्या (r) व व्यासाचे संबंध d = 2r असल्याने C = 2πr होतो. उदा., र = 7 सेमी असल्यास, d = 14 सेमी, C = (22/7) × 14 = 44 सेमी. र = 14 सेमी असल्यास, d = 28 सेमी, C = (22/7) × 28 = 88 सेमी. हे दर्शवितात की त्रिज्या वाढल्यास परीघ देखील समानुपातिक रूपाने वाढतो.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: काटकोन त्रिकोणात कर्णाची लांबी शोधण्यासाठी पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त कसे वापरते?
questions.answer: काटकोन त्रिकोणात कर्णाची लांबी शोधण्यासाठी, पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त c² = a² + b² वापरते, जिथे c कर्ण, a व b काटकोन करणाऱ्या बाजूंची लांबी आहे. त्यामुई a व b ओळखवून c शोधतो.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त कसे सत्यापित केला जातो?
questions.answer: पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त सत्यापित करण्यासाठी, काटकोन त्रिकोणाची सर्व बाजूंची लांबी मोजली जाते. त्यानंतर कर्णाच्या वर्गACHE मูล्य व इतर दोन बाजूंच्या वर्गांचा योग तुलना केला जातो. जे समान असतील, त सिद्धान्त सत्यापित होतो.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: काटकोन त्रिकोणात कर्ण सर्वात लांबी बाजू कसा होतो? कारण सांगा.
questions.answer: काटकोन त्रिकोणात कर्ण सर्वात लांबी बाजू असतो, कारण त्याच वर्गाचा मูล्य इतर दोन बाजूंच्या वर्गांचा योग असतो. दोन सकारात्मक संख्यांचा योग त्यांचे प्रत्येक व्यक्तिगत वर्गापेक्षा मोठा असतो, त्यामुई कर्णाची लांबी इतर बाजूपेक्षा मोठी असते.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: पायथागोरसचे त्रिकुट (7, 24, 25) हे बरोबर आहे का? कारण सांगा.
questions.answer: होय, पायथागोरसचे त्रिकुट (7, 24, 25) बरोबर आहे, कारण 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². त्यामुई मोठ्या संख्याचा वर्ग इतर दोन संख्यांच्या वर्गांचा योगासमान असतो, ज्यामुई हे पायथागोरसचे त्रिकुट आहे.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त फक्त काटकोन त्रिकोणावरच लागू होते का? कारण सांगा.
questions.answer: होय, पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त फक्त काटकोन त्रिकोणावरच लागू होते, कारण तो सिद्धान्त कर्णाच्या वर्गACHE मूल्य आणि इतर दोन बाजूंच्या वर्गांचा योग आधारित असतो. काटकोन त्रिकोणात फक्त एक कोण 90° असतो, ज्यामुई ही संबंध सत्य असते. इतर त्रिकोणात ही संबंध सत्य नाही.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.text: पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त काय आहे? त्याचा इतिहास, सत्यापन पद्धती व वास्तविक जीवनातील वापर सांगा.
questions.answer: पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्त सांगते की काटकोन त्रिकोणात कर्णाचा वर्ग इतर दोन बाजूंच्या वर्गांचा योग असतो. हे सिद्धान्त प्राचीन यावन गणितज्ञ पायथागोरसाने प्रथम दिला गेला, परंतु भारतातील शुल्वसूत्रे हे आधी ज्ञात होते. सिद्धान्तACHE सत्यापन काटकोन त्रिकोणाची बाजू मोजून त्यांचे वर्गांचा योग तुलना करून केला जातो. वास्तविक जीवनात हे सिद्धान्त इमारती, नकाशे, रस्ते, उंची मापणे, इत्यादी क्षेत्रात वापरला जातो. उदा. शिडीची लांबी, भिंतीची उंची, इत्यादी शोधण्यासाठी हे उपयुक्त आहे.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरणांचा समाधान करा व पूर्ण कामकाज लिहा.
questions.text: एक काटकोन त्रिकोणात दोन बाजूंची लांबी 9 सेमी व 12 सेमी आहे. कर्णाची लांबी काढा.
questions.answer: दिले अनुसार: एक बाजू (a) = 9 सेमी दुसरी बाजू (b) = 12 सेमी कर्ण (c) = ? पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्तानुसार: c² = a² + b² c² = 9² + 12² c² = 81 + 144 c² = 225 c = √225 c = 15 सेमी अतः, कर्णाची लांबी 15 सेमी आहे.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरणांचा समाधान करा व पूर्ण कामकाज लिहा.
questions.text: काटकोन त्रिकोणात कर्णाची लांबी 25 सेमी आहे व एक बाजू 7 सेमी आहे. दुसरी बाजूची लांबी काढा.
questions.answer: दिले अनुसार: कर्ण (c) = 25 सेमी एक बाजू (a) = 7 सेमी दुसरी बाजू (b) = ? पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्तानुसार: c² = a² + b² 25² = 7² + b² 625 = 49 + b² b² = 625 - 49 b² = 576 b = √576 b = 24 सेमी अतः, दुसरी बाजूची लांबी 24 सेमी आहे.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरणांचा समाधान करा व पूर्ण कामकाज लिहा.
questions.text: एक चौरसाची विकर्ण 10 सेमी आहे. चौरसाची बाजूची लांबी काढा.
questions.answer: दिले अनुसार: चौरसाची विकर्ण (d) = 10 सेमी चौरसाची बाजू (a) = ? चौरसात विकर्ण दोन काटकोन त्रिकोण बनवते, ज्या त्रिकोणात बाजू व बाजू काटकोन करणाऱ्या बाजू असतात व विकर्ण कर्ण असतो. पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्तानुसार: d² = a² + a² d² = 2a² 10² = 2a² 100 = 2a² a² = 50 a = √50 a = 5√2 सेमी ≈ 7.07 सेमी अतः, चौरसाची बाजूची लांबी 5√2 सेमी (किमत 7.07 सेमी) आहे.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरणांचा समाधान करा व पूर्ण कामकाज लिहा.
questions.text: एक आयामदीप 15 मी उंच आहे. त्याची आधार 8 मी दूर एका भितीवर टिकली आहे. दीपाचा प्रकाश भितीवर कोठे पडेल?
questions.answer: दिले अनुसार: आयामदीपची उंची (h) = 15 मी आधार भितीवरून अंतर (d) = 8 मी प्रकाश पडण्याचा उंची (h') = ? आयामदीप, आधार व भिती काटकोन त्रिकोण बनवते, ज्या त्रिकोणात उंची व आधार काटकोन करणाऱ्या बाजू असतात व प्रकाश पडण्याचा उंची कर्ण असतो. पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्तानुसार: h'² = h² + d² h'² = 15² + 8² h'² = 225 + 64 h'² = 289 h' = √289 h' = 17 मी अतः, प्रकाश 17 मी उंचीवर पडेल.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.instruction: खालील उदाहरणांचा समाधान करा व पूर्ण कामकाज लिहा.
questions.text: एक शिडी 17 मी लांबी आहे. त्याची खाल 8 मी भितीवर टिकली आहे. शिडीची डोक भितीवर किती उंचीपर्यंत पोहोचते?
questions.answer: दिले अनुसार: शिडीची लांबी (l) = 17 मी भितीवरून खालचा अंतर (d) = 8 मी भितीवर डोक उंची (h) = ? शिडी, भिती व जमीन काटकोन त्रिकोण बनवते, ज्या त्रिकोणात डोक उंची व भितीवरून खालचा अंतर काटकोन करणाऱ्या बाजू असतात व शिडीची लांबी कर्ण असतो. पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्तानुसार: l² = h² + d² 17² = h² + 8² 289 = h² + 64 h² = 289 - 64 h² = 225 h = √225 h = 15 मी अतः, शिडीची डोक भितीवर 15 मी उंचीपर्यंत पोहोचते.

questions.text: एक आयाताकार बक्सा 6 मी लांबा, 8 मी रुंदा आहे. बक्साच्या एका कोनेपर्यंत विकर्णाची लांबी काढा.
questions.answer: दिले अनुसार: बक्साची लांबी (l) = 6 मी बक्साची रुंदी (w) = 8 मी विकर्ण (d) = ? बक्साच्या आधारावर एक आयाताकार बनेल, ज्या त्रिकोणात लांबी व रुंदी काटकोन करणाऱ्या बाजू असतात व विकर्ण कर्ण असतो. पायथागोरसचे सिद्धान्तानुसार: d² = l² + w² d² = 6² + 8² d² = 36 + 64 d² = 100 d = √100 d = 10 मी अतः, बक्साच्या एका कोनेपर्यंत विकर्णाची लांबी 10 मी आहे.

questions.text: (x + y)² चा विस्तार x² + y² नाही, बरोबर x² + 2xy + y² असते, का?
questions.answer: क्योकि (x + y)² = (x + y)(x + y) = x(x + y) + y(x + y) = x² + xy + yx + y² = x² + 2xy + y². xy व yx एकत्र होऊन 2xy होतात, त्यामुळे 2xy पद आवश्यक आहे.

questions.subject: Maths

questions.answer: क्योकि (x + y)(x - y) = x(x - y) + y(x - y) = x² - xy + yx - y² = x² - y². -xy व +yx एकत्र होऊन शून्य होतात, त्यामुळे फक्त x² - y² राहते.

questions.text: Describe two adaptations in cactus that help it survive in deserts.

questions.subject: Science

questions.text: How do aquatic plants like lotus prevent rotting in water?
questions.answer: The leaves and stems of lotus have a waxy coating that prevents water from sticking and rotting. Additionally, air spaces in their stems help them float and exchange gases.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Why do polar bears have a thick layer of fat under their skin?
questions.answer: Polar bears live in extremely cold snowy regions. The thick layer of fat acts as insulation, helping to retain body heat and protect against freezing temperatures.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Why do desert animals like rats and snakes stay in burrows during the day?
questions.answer: Deserts are extremely hot during the day. Staying in cool, deep burrows helps these animals avoid overheating and reduce water loss through evaporation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Why do forest trees grow tall?
questions.answer: In forests, trees compete for sunlight. Growing tall allows them to reach the sunlight that is blocked by shorter plants and canopy layers.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.instruction: Write a short paragraph in 6-10 lines.
questions.text: Explain how adaptations help organisms survive in their habitats. Give examples from desert, aquatic, and snowy regions.
questions.answer: Adaptations are special features that help organisms survive in their environment. In deserts, plants like cactus have spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss and store water in their stems. Aquatic plants like lotus have waxy leaves and air-filled stems to float and avoid rotting. In snowy regions, animals like polar bears have thick fur and fat layers to keep warm, and their white colour provides camouflage. These adaptations develop over long periods and are essential for survival.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.instruction: Write a short paragraph in 6-10 lines.
questions.text: Describe the hierarchy of classification with an example of a mango tree.
questions.answer: Classification organizes living things into groups based on similarities. The hierarchy starts with Kingdom, then Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, and Species. For example, a mango tree belongs to Kingdom Plantae, Phylum Anthophylla, Class Dicotyledonae, Order Sapindales, Family Anacardiaceae, Genus Mangifera, and Species indica. This system helps scientists identify and study organisms systematically.

questions.answer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a scientific name consisting of two parts: the genus name and the species name.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Habitat
questions.answer: Habitat is the natural environment where an organism lives, finds food, shelter, and reproduces.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Terrestrial plants and Aquatic plants
questions.answer: Terrestrial plants grow in soil and have roots for anchorage and absorption; aquatic plants grow in water and may have air spaces for floating. Terrestrial plants have thick cuticles to prevent water loss; aquatic plants have thin, waxy leaves to allow water to slip off. Terrestrial plants rely on soil for nutrients; aquatic plants absorb dissolved nutrients directly from water. Terrestrial plants often have deep roots; aquatic plants may have reduced or fibrous roots.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Herbivores and Carnivores
questions.answer: Herbivores eat only plants; carnivores eat other animals. Herbivores have flat molars for grinding plant material; carnivores have sharp, pointed teeth for tearing flesh. Herbivores often have longer digestive tracts to digest cellulose; carnivores have shorter digestive tracts. Herbivores like deer have eyes on the sides for wide vision; carnivores like lions have eyes in front for depth perception to hunt.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Explain how the shape and structure of fish help them live in water.
questions.answer: Fish have a streamlined, spindle-shaped body that reduces resistance while swimming. Their bodies are covered with scales that protect them and aid in smooth movement. Fins help in balancing, changing direction, and propelling through water. Gills extract dissolved oxygen from water for respiration. Many fish also have an air bladder that helps them maintain buoyancy and float at different depths without sinking or rising.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
questions.text: Explain why classification of living organisms is important.
questions.answer: Classification helps us organize the vast diversity of living organisms into manageable groups. It makes it easier to study, identify, and remember different species. It shows evolutionary relationships and helps in understanding how organisms are related. Classification also avoids confusion by giving each organism a unique scientific name. It supports fields like medicine, agriculture, and conservation by organizing biological knowledge systematically.

questions.text: A student observed that in a desert, a cactus survived 30 days without water, while a rose plant died in 5 days. If the cactus stores 1500 mL of water and uses it at a constant rate, how much water does it use per day?
questions.answer: Total water stored = 1500 mL Number of days survived = 30 days Water used per day = Total water / Number of days = 1500 mL / 30 = 50 mL/day Therefore, the cactus uses 50 mL of water per day.

questions.text: In a pond, there are 20 lotus plants. Each lotus leaf has an area of 0.25 m². If the leaves cover 60% of the pond surface, what is the total surface area of the pond?
questions.answer: Area of one leaf = 0.25 m² Number of leaves = 20 Total leaf area = 20 × 0.25 = 5 m² This covers 60% of the pond. Let total pond area = x Then, 60% of x = 5 m² → 0.6x = 5 → x = 5 / 0.6 = 8.33 m² Therefore, the total surface area of the pond is approximately 8.33 m².

questions.text: What are aerial roots?
questions.answer: Aerial roots are roots that grow above the soil and absorb moisture from the air.

questions.text: What is the function of stomata in leaves?

questions.text: What is pollination?
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differentiate between tap root and fibrous root systems.
questions.answer: Tap root system has one main thick root that grows deep into the soil with smaller lateral branches, as seen in neem or carrot. Fibrous root system consists of many thin, thread-like roots of similar size arising from the base of the stem, as seen in grass or maize. Tap roots provide deep anchorage, while fibrous roots prevent soil erosion by spreading widely near the surface.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how roots of a banyan tree help it to grow and spread.
questions.answer: The banyan tree develops prop roots from its branches that grow downward into the soil. These roots provide additional mechanical support to the heavy branches. As they grow and thicken, they resemble trunks, allowing the tree to spread over a large area and appear like a small forest.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the structure of a typical flower with its four whorls.
questions.answer: A typical flower has four whorls: calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens), and gynoecium (carpels). Sepals are usually green and protect the bud. Petals are coloured and attract pollinators. Stamens produce pollen, and carpels contain the ovary where ovules develop into seeds after fertilization.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are leaves of some plants modified into spines?
questions.answer: In some plants, leaves are modified into spines to reduce water loss by minimizing surface area. Spines also protect the plant from herbivores. This adaptation is common in xerophytes like cactus and in plants like bougainvillea where stipules become spines.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the root tip covered by a root cap?
questions.answer: The root tip is covered by a root cap to protect the delicate meristematic cells from mechanical injury as the root pushes through soil particles. The root cap secretes mucilage that lubricates the path for easier growth. It also helps in sensing gravity and directing root growth downward.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do plants like maize and sugarcane have stilt roots?
questions.answer: Maize and sugarcane have stilt roots to provide additional mechanical support to their tall, slender stems. These roots arise from the lower nodes of the stem and grow obliquely into the soil, anchoring the plant firmly and preventing lodging due to wind or the weight of the shoot.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are the leaves of aquatic plants often thin and ribbon-like?
questions.answer: Aquatic plants have thin, ribbon-like leaves to reduce resistance to water currents and allow easy movement. This shape increases surface area for efficient absorption of dissolved gases and minerals from water. It also prevents damage from flowing water and allows light penetration to submerged parts.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the various types of root modifications and their functions with examples.
questions.answer: Root modifications occur to perform special functions beyond absorption and anchorage. Tap roots modify into storage roots like carrot and radish to store food. Prop roots, as in banyan, grow from branches to the soil for support. Stilt roots in maize and sugarcane arise from lower stem nodes to provide mechanical support. Pneumatophores in mangroves grow upward to obtain oxygen for respiration in waterlogged soils. Adventitious roots like those in grass help in vegetative propagation. Some roots become photosynthetic (e.g., Taeniophyllum) or form nodules for nitrogen fixation (e.g., legumes). These adaptations help plants survive in specific environmental conditions.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the structure of a leaf and describe the different types of leaf venation with examples.
questions.answer: A leaf consists of leaf-blade (lamina), petiole, leaf-base, and sometimes stipules. The lamina shows venation, which is the arrangement of veins. There are two main types: reticulate and parallel. In reticulate venation, veins form a network, as seen in peepal, mango, and rose leaves—common in dicots. In parallel venation, veins run side by side from base to apex, as in maize, grass, and lily—common in monocots. Other types include dichotomous (forking) in ferns and circinate in young fern leaves. Venation helps in transport of water, minerals, and food, and provides mechanical strength to the leaf.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants prepare their own food using carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight in the presence of chlorophyll.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define transpiration.
questions.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, mainly through stomata in leaves.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is germination?
questions.answer: Germination is the process by which a seed develops into a young plant under favourable conditions of water, oxygen, and temperature.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Differentiate between simple and compound leaves.
questions.answer: Simple leaves have a single undivided leaf blade attached to the stem by a petiole, e.g., peepal. Compound leaves have the leaf blade divided into several leaflets attached to a common stalk called rachis, e.g., neem and rose. In simple leaves, the bud is present in the axil of the leaf. In compound leaves, bud is present only at the base of the whole leaf, not in the axil of leaflets. Simple leaves show less surface area exposure, while compound leaves allow better wind passage and light penetration.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Differentiate between monocot and dicot seeds.
questions.answer: Monocot seeds have one cotyledon, e.g., maize and wheat. Dicot seeds have two cotyledons, e.g., pea and gram. Monocot seeds usually have endosperm that stores food, while in dicots, food is stored in the cotyledons. The coleoptile and coleoriza protect the plumule and radicle in monocots, which are absent in dicots. Monocot leaves show parallel venation, while dicots show reticulate venation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the structure of a root hair is suited to its function.
questions.answer: Root hairs are thin, tubular extensions of epidermal cells that greatly increase the surface area for absorption. Their thin walls allow easy movement of water and minerals into the cell. They grow in the region just behind the root tip where cells are matured but still active. The large number of root hairs enhances contact with soil particles. This structure makes them efficient in absorbing water and nutrients from the soil.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the process of fertilization in a flower after pollination.
questions.answer: After pollination, pollen grains germinate on the stigma and grow a pollen tube down the style. The tube carries two male gametes toward the ovary. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote, which develops into the embryo. The other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm, which nourishes the embryo. This process is called double fertilization. The ovary then develops into a fruit, and ovules into seeds.

questions.text: Why is it easier to swim in sea water than in fresh water?

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how atmospheric pressure is demonstrated using a syringe.
questions.answer: When the piston of a closed syringe is pulled out, the air inside expands, reducing its pressure. The higher outside atmospheric pressure then pushes the piston back in, showing that air exerts pressure in all directions.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How does a straw fountain work based on Bernoulli’s principle?
questions.answer: Blowing air through a straw reduces pressure at its tip. The higher atmospheric pressure inside the cup pushes water up the straw, creating a fountain. This demonstrates that increased air velocity decreases pressure.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is soil testing important for farmers?
questions.answer: Soil testing helps determine pH, nutrient content, and texture, enabling farmers to choose suitable crops and apply correct fertilizers to improve yield and maintain soil fertility.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: List three uses of water based on its properties.
questions.answer: Water is used for generating electricity (from height), as a coolant in engines, and as a universal solvent in biological and industrial processes.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does the level of ice rise above the original water level when water freezes?
questions.answer: When water freezes into ice, its volume increases due to the open hexagonal structure of ice. This expansion causes the ice level to rise above the original water level.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease with altitude?
questions.answer: Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because the weight of air above reduces as we go higher, resulting in fewer air molecules exerting force per unit area.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do water droplets form on the outside of a glass containing ice-cold water?
questions.answer: The cold surface of the glass cools the surrounding air, reducing its capacity to hold water vapour. The excess vapour condenses into liquid water droplets on the glass surface.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the properties of air that make it essential for life on Earth.
questions.answer: Air is essential for life as it provides oxygen for respiration, contains nitrogen for plant growth, and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. It transmits sound, protects from harmful solar radiation, and regulates temperature via the greenhouse effect. Air also enables flight and wind-powered energy. Its pressure supports barometric functions in living beings. Being a homogeneous mixture of gases, it ensures uniform availability of components. Air’s ability to dissolve gases supports aquatic life. Thus, air sustains life through multiple interconnected properties.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the anomalous behaviour of water and its importance in aquatic ecosystems.
questions.answer: Water exhibits anomalous behaviour by reaching maximum density at 4°C and expanding upon freezing. This causes ice to float, insulating water below and allowing aquatic life to survive in winter. In lakes, colder water stays on top while denser 4°C water sinks, creating a stable environment. Without this, lakes would freeze solid, killing ecosystems. The property also drives ocean currents and nutrient mixing. Hence, anomalous behaviour of water is vital for preserving life in cold climates.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State the difference between the following.
questions.text: Differentiate between sandy soil and clay soil.
questions.answer: Sandy soil has large particles, drains water quickly, is poorly fertile, and easy to plough. Clay soil has fine particles, retains water, is highly fertile but hard to plough due to stickiness when wet and hardness when dry.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State the difference between the following.
questions.text: Differentiate between evaporation and boiling.
questions.answer: Evaporation occurs at the surface of liquid at any temperature, is slow, and causes cooling. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature, is rapid, and requires external heat.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how air pressure decreases with increase in velocity of air, with an example.
questions.answer: According to Bernoulli’s principle, as the velocity of air increases, its pressure decreases. This happens because moving air transfers energy to motion, reducing the energy available for pressure. For example, in a straw fountain, blowing air reduces pressure at the straw’s tip, allowing atmospheric pressure to push water up. Similarly, airplane wings are shaped so air moves faster above, creating lift due to lower pressure. This principle also explains why curtains bulge out when wind blows outside.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why soil structure is important for plant growth.
questions.answer: Good soil structure allows proper aeration, enabling roots to respire and absorb oxygen. It ensures adequate water drainage, preventing root rot while retaining sufficient moisture. It allows easy root penetration and growth. It also supports microbial activity that enriches soil with nutrients. Thus, soil structure directly affects plant health, yield, and sustainability.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How does chemosynthesis differ from photosynthesis?
questions.answer: Chemosynthesis uses chemical energy from inorganic compounds instead of sunlight to produce food.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: State one advantage of symbiotic nutrition for fungi.
questions.answer: Fungi receive carbohydrates from their plant partners, supporting their growth.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is the main function of the xylem?
questions.answer: Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals from roots to aerial parts of the plant.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how lightning contributes to soil fertility.
questions.answer: Lightning causes atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen to combine forming nitric oxide, which later becomes nitric acid in rainwater; this acid reacts with soil minerals to form nitrates that plants can absorb, enhancing soil fertility.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the steps of holozoic nutrition in animals.
questions.answer: First, ingestion – food is taken in; second, digestion – complex food is broken down into simple molecules; third, absorption – nutrients pass into the bloodstream; fourth, assimilation – cells use nutrients for energy, growth and repair; finally, egestion – undigested waste is expelled.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: List two adaptations of parasitic plants that help them obtain nutrients from hosts.
questions.answer: They develop haustoria that penetrate host tissues to draw water and nutrients, and they often lack chlorophyll, reducing the need for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are the visible symptoms of nitrogen deficiency in plants?
questions.answer: Leaves become pale or yellowish (chlorosis), growth is stunted, and older leaves may show necrotic spots.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do insect‑ivorous plants grow in nitrogen‑poor habitats?
questions.answer: In nitrogen‑deficient soils, these plants supplement their nitrogen intake by trapping insects, which provide a rich source of nitrogen when digested.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the phloem located towards the outer part of the vascular bundle?
questions.answer: Being peripheral protects the delicate sieve‑tube elements from mechanical damage and allows efficient transport of sugars to growing tissues located near the outer regions of the stem.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do saprophytic fungi secrete enzymes onto dead material before absorption?
questions.answer: Enzymes break down complex organic polymers into simpler soluble molecules that the fungal hyphae can then absorb for nutrition.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Summarize the importance of micronutrients in plant growth.
questions.answer: Micronutrients such as iron, manganese, zinc and copper are required in trace amounts but are vital for enzyme activation, chlorophyll synthesis and hormone production. Deficiencies lead to symptoms like chlorosis, stunted growth, and reduced yield. Supplying these nutrients through soil amendments or foliar sprays ensures healthy metabolic functions and optimal crop productivity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the role of symbiotic relationships in nutrient acquisition for plants.
questions.answer: Symbiotic relationships, like those between legumes and rhizobium bacteria or mycorrhizal fungi and plant roots, enhance nutrient acquisition. Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen into forms usable by the plant, while mycorrhizae increase the root surface area, improving uptake of phosphorus and water. Both interactions reduce the plant’s dependence on soil nutrient availability and promote better growth and resilience.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define autotrophic nutrition.
questions.answer: Autotrophic nutrition is the mode of obtaining food in which an organism synthesizes its own organic substances from inorganic materials, typically using light energy (photosynthesis) or chemical energy (chemosynthesis).

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define heterotrophic nutrition.
questions.answer: Heterotrophic nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain organic food by consuming other living or dead organisms, as they cannot produce their own food.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define symbiotic nutrition.
questions.answer: Symbiotic nutrition is a mutual relationship where two different organisms live together and exchange nutrients, each benefiting from the other's metabolic capabilities.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differences between xylem and phloem.
questions.answer: 1) Xylem transports water and minerals upward; phloem transports organic food (sugars) both upward and downward. 2) Xylem cells are dead at maturity forming hollow tubes; phloem cells are living sieve elements. 3) Xylem movement is driven by transpiration pull and root pressure; phloem movement is driven by pressure flow generated by loading and unloading of sugars. 4) Xylem is located centrally in stems; phloem is situated towards the outer side of the vascular bundle.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differences between parasitic and saprophytic nutrition.
questions.answer: 1) Parasitic nutrition involves a living host from which the parasite extracts nutrients; saprophytic nutrition uses dead organic matter. 2) Parasites often cause harm to the host; saprophytes aid decomposition without harming living organisms. 3) Parasites may have specialized structures like haustoria; saprophytes secrete extracellular enzymes to break down material. 4) Parasites are usually more host‑specific, whereas saprophytes can act on a wide range of dead substrates.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis begins when chlorophyll absorbs sunlight, exciting electrons in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. This energy drives the light‑dependent reactions, producing ATP and NADPH while splitting water to release oxygen. In the Calvin cycle (light‑independent reactions), ATP and NADPH are used to fix carbon dioxide into glucose, a stable chemical energy store. Thus, light energy is transformed into the chemical bonds of glucose.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the process of nitrogen fixation by soil bacteria.
questions.answer: Soil bacteria such as Rhizobium and Azotobacter possess the enzyme nitrogenase, which reduces atmospheric N₂ to ammonia (NH₃) under anaerobic conditions. In legume root nodules, Rhizobium converts N₂ to ammonia, which is then assimilated into amino acids. Free‑living Azotobacter performs a similar conversion in the soil, making nitrates available for plant uptake. This biological fixation supplies essential nitrogen for protein synthesis in plants.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: A plant leaf absorbs 8 µmol of CO₂ per hour during photosynthesis. If the leaf produces glucose with a 1:6 molar ratio of CO₂ to glucose, how many µmol of glucose are formed in 5 hours? Show your calculation.
questions.answer: CO₂ absorbed in 5 h = 8 µmol/h × 5 h = 40 µmol. For every 6 CO₂ molecules, 1 glucose molecule is formed, so glucose formed = 40 µmol ÷ 6 = 6.67 µmol (approx).

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: A farmer applies 50 kg of a fertilizer containing 20% nitrogen. How many kilograms of nitrogen are added to the soil? Show your work.
questions.answer: Nitrogen content = 20% of 50 kg = 0.20 × 50 = 10 kg. Therefore, 10 kg of nitrogen are added.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how improper storage leads to food spoilage.
questions.answer: Improper storage, such as keeping food in damp or warm places, promotes the growth of mould, bacteria, and insects. This leads to changes in colour, odour, and texture, making the food unsafe and reducing its nutritional value.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are the signs that indicate food has spoiled?
questions.answer: Spoiled food may show changes in colour, develop a foul odour, become slimy or sticky in texture, taste sour or bitter, and may have visible mould or insect infestation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How does pasteurization help in preserving milk?
questions.answer: Pasteurization involves heating milk to about 80°C for 15 minutes and then cooling it rapidly. This process kills harmful microbes without significantly affecting the taste or nutritional value, thus keeping milk safe for longer.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Suggest two ways to prevent food wastage at home.
questions.answer: We can prevent food wastage by cooking only the required amount of food and storing leftovers properly for reuse. Additionally, buying groceries based on actual need and checking expiry dates before purchase helps avoid excess and spoilage.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Give reason for the following in 3-4 sentences.
questions.text: Why should we not consume adulterated food materials?
questions.answer: Adulterated food may contain harmful substances like stones, chemicals, or low-quality materials that can cause abdominal discomfort, poisoning, or long-term organ damage. Some adulterants are carcinogenic and may lead to cancer with prolonged consumption. Consuming such food puts our health at serious risk, especially children and the elderly. Therefore, it is essential to avoid adulterated food to maintain good health and prevent diseases.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Give reason for the following in 3-4 sentences.
questions.text: Why is food preservation important?
questions.answer: Food preservation prevents spoilage caused by microbes, enzymes, and environmental factors, thereby extending the shelf-life of food. It helps retain nutritional value, taste, and safety, reducing the risk of food-borne illnesses. Preservation also reduces food wastage, ensuring more people can be fed with the available supply. It is especially important in areas with limited access to fresh food or during emergencies.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Give reason for the following in 3-4 sentences.
questions.text: Why do we store grains in airtight containers?
questions.answer: Storing grains in airtight containers prevents moisture and air from entering, which reduces the risk of fungal growth and insect infestation. It also protects the grains from contamination by dust, pests, and rodents. This method helps maintain the quality, nutritional value, and germination capacity of seeds for a longer period. Airtight storage is a simple yet effective way of food protection at home.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Food adulteration
questions.answer: Food adulteration is the act of adding inferior, harmful, or unnecessary substances to food, or removing valuable components, which reduces its quality and poses health risks.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Food preservation
questions.answer: Food preservation refers to the use of various techniques such as freezing, drying, pasteurization, or adding preservatives to prevent spoilage and keep food safe and edible for an extended period.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Qualitative wastage of food
questions.answer: Qualitative wastage of food refers to the loss of nutritional value, taste, texture, or safety of food due to improper handling, over-cooking, or excessive use of preservatives, even if the quantity remains unchanged.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State the difference between the following in 3-4 points.
questions.text: Food protection and food preservation
questions.answer: Food protection focuses on preventing spoilage by controlling external factors like microbes, pests, and contamination during handling and storage. Food preservation involves treating food with methods like heating, drying, or adding chemicals to inhibit internal biological and chemical changes. Protection is about safeguarding food from outside harm, while preservation aims to slow down internal deterioration. Both work together to ensure food safety and longevity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State the difference between the following in 3-4 points.
questions.text: Quantitative and qualitative wastage of food
questions.answer: Quantitative wastage refers to the loss of food in terms of amount or weight, such as spoilage due to poor storage or overproduction. Qualitative wastage occurs when food loses its nutritional value, taste, or safety without a significant reduction in quantity, for example, over-cooking vegetables. Quantitative wastage can be measured in kilograms, while qualitative wastage is assessed by quality degradation. Both types reduce the effective availability of nutritious food.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how irradiation helps in food preservation.
questions.answer: Irradiation exposes food to ionizing radiation such as gamma rays, X-rays, or high-energy electrons. This radiation destroys microbes, insects, and their eggs by damaging their DNA, preventing reproduction and spoilage. It also slows down sprouting in potatoes and onions, increasing their shelf-life. The process does not make the food radioactive and leaves no harmful residue. Irradiation is used for spices, onions, and potatoes to ensure long-term preservation without affecting taste or nutrition significantly.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the role of FSSAI in ensuring food safety in India.
questions.answer: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is responsible for setting science-based standards for food articles and regulating their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale, and import. It ensures that food is safe, wholesome, and fit for human consumption. FSSAI also monitors food adulteration, conducts surveillance, and creates awareness about safe food practices. It mandates labeling with manufacturing and expiry dates, and licensing of food businesses. Through these measures, FSSAI protects public health and promotes food safety across the country.

questions.answer: Rice bought per month = 5 kg Spoilage per month = 10% of 5 kg = 0.10 × 5 = 0.5 kg Spoilage per year = 0.5 kg × 12 months = 6 kg Therefore, 6 kg of rice is wasted in a year due to spoilage.

questions.answer: Total mixture = 10 litres milk + 2 litres water = 12 litres Pure milk = 10 litres Percentage of pure milk = (10 / 12) × 100 = 83.33% Therefore, 83.33% of the mixture is pure milk.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why standard units are necessary for measurement.
questions.answer: Standard units are necessary to ensure consistency and accuracy in measurements. Without them, measurements would vary from person to person and place to place, leading to confusion and errors in trade, science, and daily life.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Give two examples of vector quantities and explain why they are vectors.
questions.answer: Displacement and velocity are vector quantities because they require both magnitude and direction for complete description. For example, a displacement of 5 km towards north or a velocity of 60 km/h towards east.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How does the weight of an object vary from the poles to the equator?
questions.answer: The weight of an object is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator due to the Earth's shape and rotation. The polar radius is smaller than the equatorial radius, so gravitational force is stronger at the poles. Additionally, the centrifugal force due to rotation is maximum at the equator, reducing effective weight.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is standardization of weights and measures?
questions.answer: Standardization is the process of checking and adjusting weighing and measuring instruments against approved standards to ensure accuracy. It is done periodically by government authorities to prevent fraud and ensure fair trade.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is it not proper to measure quantities by using body parts as units?
questions.answer: Body parts vary in size from person to person, so measurements using them are not consistent or reliable. This leads to errors and lack of uniformity in measurements.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is it necessary to get weights and measures standardized at regular intervals?
questions.answer: Instruments can wear out, get damaged, or be tampered with over time, leading to inaccurate measurements. Regular standardization ensures they remain accurate and trustworthy.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is weight considered a vector quantity?
questions.answer: Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object, and force has both magnitude and direction (towards the centre of the Earth). Hence, weight is a vector quantity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the importance of accurate measurement in daily life and mention the devices used for measuring mass, length, and time.
questions.answer: Accurate measurement is essential in daily life for cooking, buying goods, construction, and health monitoring. It ensures fairness in trade, safety in engineering, and correctness in experiments. For mass, we use beam balance or digital scale; for length, metre scale or measuring tape; for time, stopwatch or clock. Standardized devices give reliable results, preventing errors and losses.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the International System of Units (SI) and list the fundamental units with their symbols.
questions.answer: The International System of Units (SI) is the modern form of the metric system, used globally for scientific and technical measurements. It is based on seven fundamental units. These are: metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature, ampere (A) for electric current, mole (mol) for amount of substance, and candela (cd) for luminous intensity. SI ensures uniformity in measurements worldwide.

questions.answer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilogram, and is constant everywhere. Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts the object, measured in newton, and varies with location due to changes in gravitational acceleration.

questions.text: Scalar and vector quantities
questions.answer: Scalar quantities have only magnitude (e.g., mass, temperature), while vector quantities have both magnitude and direction (e.g., weight, velocity). Scalars are added algebraically, vectors require geometric or vector addition.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the need for standardized units in measurement.
questions.answer: Standardized units are essential to ensure that measurements are consistent and comparable across different places and times. Without standardization, confusion would arise in trade, science, and daily activities. For example, if one person uses hand-span and another uses foot-span to measure cloth, the measurements would not match. Standard units like metre, kilogram, and second are universally accepted and maintained by international bodies.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the weight of an object changes with altitude and why.
questions.answer: The weight of an object decreases with increasing altitude above sea level. This is because gravitational force decreases with distance from the Earth's centre. At higher altitudes, the object is farther from the Earth's centre, so the gravitational pull is weaker, resulting in lower weight. For example, an object weighs less on a mountain than at sea level.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differentiate between distance and displacement.
questions.answer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled by a body, irrespective of direction, and is a scalar quantity. Displacement is the shortest distance from the initial to the final position of a body in a particular direction and is a vector quantity. Distance can never be zero if motion occurs, but displacement can be zero if the body returns to its starting point.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how force is related to acceleration.
questions.answer: Force produces acceleration in a body; the greater the force applied, the greater the acceleration produced, provided the mass remains constant. This relationship is given by Newton's second law: F = m × a. If no force acts on a body, its acceleration is zero, meaning it moves with constant velocity or remains at rest.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is instantaneous velocity? How is it different from average velocity?
questions.answer: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity of a body at a particular instant of time. Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time taken. Instantaneous velocity can vary at different points, while average velocity gives an overall measure for the entire journey.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Give two examples where friction is useful and two where it is harmful.
questions.answer: Friction is useful in walking and applying brakes in vehicles. It is harmful as it causes wear and tear of machine parts and reduces efficiency by producing heat.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does a ball rolling on the ground eventually come to a stop?
questions.answer: A ball rolling on the ground comes to a stop due to the force of friction acting opposite to its motion, which reduces its velocity to zero.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is it easier to pull a lawn roller than to push it?
questions.answer: When pulling, the vertical component of the applied force reduces the normal reaction, thereby decreasing friction; when pushing, it increases the normal reaction and hence friction.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does a passenger lean forward when a moving bus stops suddenly?
questions.answer: Due to inertia of motion, the passenger tends to continue moving forward even when the bus stops, causing a forward lean.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Force
questions.answer: Force is an external agent that can change or tend to change the state of rest or uniform motion of a body, or change its shape or size.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write the difference between the following.
questions.text: Speed and velocity
questions.answer: Speed is the distance travelled per unit time and is a scalar quantity. Velocity is the displacement per unit time and is a vector quantity. Speed has only magnitude, while velocity has both magnitude and direction.

Displacement is the shortest distance from initial to final position in a specific direction, and is vector. Distance ≥ |displacement|, and displacement can be zero while distance cannot be zero if motion occurs.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain Newton's first law of motion with examples.
questions.answer: Newton's first law states that a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force. This property is called inertia. For example, a book on a table remains at rest until someone pushes it. Similarly, a moving car continues to move forward with the same speed if brakes are not applied, assuming no friction. When a bus starts suddenly, passengers fall backward due to inertia of rest. When it stops suddenly, they fall forward due to inertia of motion. This law defines the concept of force as that which changes the state of motion.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how work done depends on the angle between force and displacement.
questions.answer: Work done is given by W = F s cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. When θ = 0°, cosθ = 1, and work is maximum and positive. When θ = 90°, cosθ = 0, and no work is done. When θ = 180°, cosθ = -1, and work is negative, meaning work is done against the force. Thus, work depends on the direction of force relative to displacement.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A force of 20 N acts on a body and displaces it by 5 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.
questions.answer: Given: Force (F) = 20 N, Displacement (s) = 5 m, and the displacement is in the direction of force, so θ = 0°. We know, Work (W) = F × s × cosθ Substituting the values: W = 20 × 5 × cos 0° Since cos 0° = 1, W = 20 × 5 × 1 = 100 J Therefore, the work done is 100 Joules.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with full working.
questions.text: A body of mass 2 kg is moving with a velocity of 3 m/s. A force acts on it for 2 seconds and increases its velocity to 7 m/s. Find the acceleration and the force applied.
questions.answer: Given: mass (m) = 2 kg, initial velocity (u) = 3 m/s, final velocity (v) = 7 m/s, time (t) = 2 s Acceleration (a) = (v - u) / t = (7 - 3) / 2 = 4 / 2 = 2 m/s² Using Newton's second law: F = m × a = 2 × 2 = 4 N Therefore, acceleration = 2 m/s² and force applied = 4 N.

questions.text: What is the cause of lightning according to the chapter?
questions.answer: Lightning occurs due to the discharge of built-up electric charge between clouds and the ground or between clouds.

questions.subject: Science

questions.answer: The copper strip conducts the electric charge from the cloud to the ground safely.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are gold leaves used in an electroscope?
questions.answer: Gold leaves are used because they are very light and conductive, so they diverge noticeably when charged.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how a plastic comb gets charged when rubbed with hair and why it attracts small pieces of paper.
questions.answer: When the comb is rubbed with hair, electrons transfer from the hair to the comb, giving the comb a negative charge. When brought near neutral paper, the negative charge repels electrons in the paper, making the near side positive. The attraction between the negatively charged comb and the induced positive charge in the paper causes the paper to move toward the comb.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the process of charging by induction using a balloon and a wall.
questions.answer: When a rubbed balloon (negatively charged) is brought near a wall, it repels electrons in the wall’s surface, making that area positively charged. The attraction between the negatively charged balloon and the induced positive charge on the wall causes the balloon to stick. No transfer of charge occurs; only rearrangement of charges in the wall.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are two harmful effects of lightning and one beneficial effect mentioned in the chapter?
questions.answer: Lightning can cause fires, damage to buildings, and harm or kill living beings due to intense heat and electric current. A beneficial effect is that it helps form nitrogen oxides, which enrich soil fertility when dissolved in rainwater.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why a charged object can attract an uncharged object.
questions.answer: A charged object induces opposite charges in the near side of an uncharged object and like charges on the far side. Since the force of attraction between opposite charges is stronger than the repulsion between like charges (due to shorter distance), there is a net attraction.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the upper end of a lightning conductor made pointed?
questions.answer: The pointed end increases the electric field strength, making it easier for charge to leak off or facilitate ionization of air, allowing the conductor to safely discharge built-up charge from the cloud.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are coal and salt placed in the pit of a lightning conductor?
questions.answer: Coal and salt increase the conductivity of the soil, helping to dissipate the electric charge quickly into the ground and reduce resistance.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does a charged balloon eventually fall off the wall after sticking for some time?
questions.answer: Over time, charge leaks from the balloon and the wall through the air or moisture, neutralizing the induced charge, so the attraction ceases and the balloon falls due to gravity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the construction and working of a lightning conductor with the help of a labelled diagram.
questions.answer: A lightning conductor consists of a pointed copper rod at the top of a building, connected to a long copper strip that runs down the building and is buried in the ground. The underground end is connected to a copper plate placed in a pit filled with coal and salt. When a negatively charged cloud passes over, it induces a positive charge on the pointed tip. The strong electric field allows charge to leak onto the conductor, which safely carries it to the ground. The coal and salt enhance soil conductivity for rapid charge dispersal.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the generation of static electricity by friction and mention two precautions to be taken while performing related experiments.
questions.answer: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons may transfer from one to the other due to differences in their affinity for electrons. The material gaining electrons becomes negatively charged, and the one losing electrons becomes positively charged. This charge remains as static electricity. Precautions: perform experiments in dry weather to prevent charge leakage, and avoid touching the charged object with hands to prevent discharging through the body.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Electric charge
questions.answer: Electric charge is an intrinsic property of subatomic particles that causes them to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field. It exists in two types: positive and negative.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Static electricity
questions.answer: Static electricity is the electric charge produced by friction, which remains on the surface of an object for a short duration and does not flow as a current.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Lightning conductor
questions.answer: A lightning conductor is a metallic rod installed on tall buildings to safely guide the electric charge from lightning into the ground, thereby protecting the structure from damage.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Conductor and Insulator
questions.answer: Conductors allow easy flow of electric charge (e.g., metals), while insulators resist the flow of charge (e.g., rubber, plastic). Conductors have free electrons; insulators have electrons tightly bound. Charging a conductor by friction is difficult as charge spreads and leaks; insulators retain charge on the rubbed area. Conductors are used in wires; insulators are used for coating wires and making handles of tools.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Like charges and Unlike charges
questions.answer: Like charges repel each other, while unlike charges attract each other. Two positive or two negative charges are like; a positive and a negative are unlike. Like charges increase potential energy when brought closer; unlike charges decrease it. Repulsion is used to test if an object is charged; attraction can occur between charged and neutral objects.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How does rubbing a balloon on hair make it stick to a wall?
questions.answer: Rubbing the balloon on hair transfers electrons from the hair to the balloon, giving the balloon a net negative charge. When brought near the wall, the negative charge repels electrons in the wall’s surface, making that region positively charged. The attraction between the negatively charged balloon and the induced positive charge on the wall causes the balloon to stick. This is an example of charging by induction. The effect is temporary as charge slowly leaks off.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What happens inside a cloud during a thunderstorm that leads to lightning?
questions.answer: Due to vigorous updrafts and collisions between ice particles, the top of the cloud becomes positively charged and the bottom negatively charged. This charge separation creates a strong electric field between the cloud and the ground. When the voltage becomes high enough, the air ionizes, creating a conductive path. A massive discharge of electrons occurs as lightning, neutralizing the charge difference. The sudden energy release produces heat, light, and thunder.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A polythene rod rubbed with wool gains a charge of 4.8 × 10⁻⁹ C. If the charge of one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, how many electrons have been transferred to the rod?
questions.answer: Number of electrons = Total charge / Charge per electron = (4.8 × 10⁻⁹) / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = (4.8 / 1.6) × 10⁻⁹⁺¹⁹ = 3 × 10¹⁰ = 30,000,000,000 electrons Therefore, 30 billion electrons have been transferred to the rod.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: If 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons are removed from a neutral object, what is the net charge on the object? (Charge of electron = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.answer: Total charge removed = Number of electrons × Charge per electron = (6.25 × 10¹⁸) × (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = (6.25 × 1.6) × 10¹⁸⁻¹⁹ = 10 × 10⁻¹ = 1.0 C Since electrons (negative charge) are removed, the object has a net positive charge. Therefore, the net charge on the object is +1.0 C.

questions.answer: To reflect heat radiation and reduce heat loss.

questions.answer: Because copper is the best conductor of heat among the three metals used.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What causes land breeze at night?
questions.answer: Land cools faster than sea at night, so air moves from land to sea, creating land breeze.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how a thermos flask keeps a hot liquid hot for a long time.
questions.answer: A thermos flask has double walls with a vacuum between them, which prevents heat loss by conduction and convection. The inner walls are silvered to reflect heat radiation, minimizing loss by radiation. The lid is also insulated, reducing heat escape from the top.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are houses in Rajasthan painted white?
questions.answer: White colour reflects most of the heat radiation from the sun, keeping the houses cooler inside. This helps in maintaining a comfortable temperature during hot summers. It is a practical application of the property of colours in relation to heat absorption.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why convection does not occur when heating water from the top in a test tube.
questions.answer: When water is heated from the top, the hot water becomes less dense and stays at the top, while the colder, denser water remains at the bottom. Since there is no downward movement of cooler water to replace the hot water, convection currents cannot form. Thus, heat transfer by convection does not occur.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is mercury used in thermometers?
questions.answer: Mercury is used in thermometers because it expands uniformly and visibly with temperature changes. It is a good conductor of heat, does not stick to the glass tube, and remains liquid over a wide range of temperatures. These properties make it ideal for accurate temperature measurement.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do we feel warmer when we come close to a fire?
questions.answer: We feel warmer near a fire because heat is transferred to our body mainly by radiation. The fire emits infrared rays that travel through the air and are absorbed by our skin and clothes, increasing our temperature. Unlike conduction or convection, radiation does not require a medium and can travel through vacuum or air.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the outer coat of penguins in Antarctica black?
questions.answer: The black colour of the penguins' outer coat helps absorb more heat radiation from the sun and the surroundings. This aids in maintaining their body temperature in the extremely cold environment of Antarctica. Black being a good absorber of heat is an adaptation for survival in cold climates.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are heaters placed near the floor and air conditioners near the ceiling in a room?
questions.answer: Heaters are placed near the floor because hot air rises due to convection, warming the room from the bottom up. Air conditioners are placed near the ceiling because cold air sinks, allowing cool air to flow downward and cool the room efficiently. This placement ensures effective distribution of temperature through convection currents.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Conduction of heat
questions.answer: Conduction of heat is the transfer of heat from the hotter part to the colder part of an object through direct contact of its particles, without the actual movement of the particles from their positions.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Radiation
questions.answer: Radiation is the transfer of heat from a hot body to a cold body without heating the medium in between, and it does not require any material medium for its propagation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Expansion of solids
questions.answer: Expansion of solids is the increase in the size or volume of a solid substance when it is heated, due to the increase in the average distance between its constituent particles.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write three differences between the following.
questions.text: Conduction and Convection
questions.answer: Conduction occurs mainly in solids through particle vibration, while convection occurs in liquids and gases due to actual movement of heated particles. Conduction does not require the medium to move, whereas convection relies on the bulk movement of the medium. In conduction, heat transfers from particle to particle; in convection, heated particles themselves carry heat from one place to another.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write three differences between the following.
questions.text: Conduction and Radiation
questions.answer: Conduction requires a material medium for heat transfer, while radiation can occur even in a vacuum. In conduction, heat transfers through direct contact of particles; in radiation, heat transfers via electromagnetic waves. Conduction is a slow process, whereas radiation travels at the speed of light.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how sea breeze is formed during the day.
questions.answer: During the day, the land heats up faster than the sea due to differences in specific heat capacity. The air above the land becomes hot, expands, and rises, creating a low-pressure area. Meanwhile, the air above the sea remains relatively cool and dense, creating a high-pressure area. To balance the pressure, cool air from the sea moves towards the land, forming a sea breeze. This process continues as long as the land is hotter than the sea.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why the pins fall at different times from the copper, aluminium and steel bars in the conduction experiment.
questions.answer: The pins fall at different times because the rate of heat conduction varies with the material. Copper has the highest thermal conductivity, so heat travels fastest through it, causing the pin to fall first. Aluminium conducts heat slower than copper but faster than steel, so its pin falls next. Steel has the lowest thermal conductivity among the three, so heat reaches its pin last, causing it to fall last. This shows that conduction depends on the nature of the material.

questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A metal ball of diameter 2 cm just passes through a metal ring. When the ball is heated, its diameter increases to 2.02 cm. Calculate the increase in diameter and the percentage increase in diameter.
questions.answer: Original diameter = 2 cm Increased diameter = 2.02 cm Increase in diameter = 2.02 - 2 = 0.02 cm Percentage increase = (Increase / Original) × 100 = (0.02 / 2) × 100 = 1% Answer: Increase in diameter = 0.02 cm, Percentage increase = 1%

questions.text: The level of water in a glass tube rises by 5 cm when the temperature increases from 20°C to 50°C. Calculate the rise in water level per degree Celsius.
questions.answer: Temperature change = 50°C - 20°C = 30°C Rise in water level = 5 cm Rise per °C = 5 cm / 30 = 0.1667 cm/°C ≈ 0.17 cm/°C Answer: The water level rises by approximately 0.17 cm for each 1°C rise in temperature.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are the effects of a volcanic eruption?
questions.answer: Volcanic eruptions lead to the collection of lava, ash, and hot mud on the earth's surface, forming mountains and hills. They pollute the atmosphere with ash and gases, often cause rainfall, increase temperature due to hot gases, and can bury forests and settlements under hot mud.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What measures can be taken to deal with famine?
questions.answer: To deal with famine, we should plan water usage and reuse, conserve water through harvesting at local level, plant trees on a large scale to prevent deforestation, and make appropriate plans based on weather forecasts.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What precautions should be taken during a thunderstorm to avoid lightning strike?
questions.answer: During a thunderstorm, one should not stand on open ground, under a tree, or near electric poles. Avoid using wired fences, mobile phones, or electrical appliances. If on a two-wheeler or boat, get off immediately and seek shelter in a pucca house or stand on dry insulating material like wood or plastic sheet with feet together and crouched low.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are the effects of flood?
questions.answer: Floods cause large-scale loss of life and property, damage to buildings and infrastructure, uprooting of trees, traffic obstructions, and disruption of normal life. They also lead to soil erosion and spread of water-borne diseases.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why should we not gather in one place during a thunderstorm?
questions.answer: We should not gather in one place during a thunderstorm because if lightning strikes, it can affect multiple people at once, increasing the risk of mass casualties. Keeping distance reduces the chance of current passing through several individuals.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is a pucca house considered the safest place during lightning?
questions.answer: A pucca house is considered safe during lightning because it is made of non-conductive materials like bricks and cement, and if equipped with a lightning conductor, it safely directs the electric charge to the ground, protecting the occupants.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do tsunami waves increase in height as they approach the coast?
questions.answer: Tsunami waves increase in height near the coast because the ocean depth decreases, causing the wave speed to reduce while the energy remains constant, which results in a significant increase in wave height.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define famine.
questions.answer: Famine is the condition that arises due to long-term and severe scarcity of foodgrains and water.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define cloudburst.
questions.answer: A cloudburst is a sudden and intense rainfall over a small geographical area, occurring at a rate of 100 mm per hour or more due to rapid condensation of water vapour in clouds.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define tsunami.
questions.answer: A tsunami is a series of ocean waves generated by the displacement of a large volume of water, typically due to an earthquake, volcanic eruption, or landslide under the sea.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Difference between flood and tsunami.
questions.answer: Flood is caused by excessive rainfall or overflow of rivers affecting land areas, while tsunami is caused by undersea earthquakes or volcanic eruptions. Floods develop slowly over hours or days, whereas tsunami waves travel at high speed (800-900 km/h) and strike suddenly. Floods mainly affect river plains and low-lying areas, while tsunami impacts coastal regions with massive wave heights. Floods can be predicted with weather forecasts, but tsunami requires early warning systems based on seismic activity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Difference between lightning and cloudburst.
questions.answer: Lightning is an electrical discharge between clouds or cloud and ground, while cloudburst is a meteorological phenomenon of sudden heavy rainfall. Lightning occurs due to static electricity buildup and lasts for a fraction of a second, whereas cloudburst lasts for minutes to hours. Lightning produces thunder and can cause fires or electrocution, while cloudburst leads to flooding and soil erosion. Lightning can be seen as a flash, while cloudburst is observed as intense rain over a small area.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how drought leads to famine.
questions.answer: Drought causes prolonged absence of rainfall, leading to failure of crops and shortage of fodder for animals. This results in scarcity of foodgrains and water in the region. As food production drops, prices rise and availability decreases, especially for the poor. Over time, the stored food gets exhausted, and without relief, people face hunger and malnutrition. If the drought continues and no aid is provided, the condition escalates into famine, affecting large populations.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the measures to prevent loss of life due to lightning.
questions.answer: To prevent loss of life due to lightning, one should avoid open fields, tall trees, and high ground during thunderstorms. Stay away from electric poles, telephone towers, and wired fences as they can conduct electricity. If outdoors, seek shelter in a pucca house or vehicle; if caught in open, crouch low with feet together on insulating material like dry wood or plastic sheet. Do not use mobile phones or electrical appliances connected to power. Swimmers and boaters should leave water immediately. Installing lightning conductors on tall buildings helps safely ground the electric charge.
