questions.subject: Science
questions.text: List the five levels of structural organization in living organisms, in correct order.
questions.answer: The five levels are: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism. Cells combine to form tissues, tissues form organs, organs work together in organ systems, and organ systems make up the whole organism.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Mention any three useful roles of microorganisms in daily life.
questions.answer: Microorganisms help in making curd and bread through fermentation, decompose organic waste into manure, and are used in the production of antibiotics and vaccines.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differentiate between plant and animal cells based on the presence of cell wall and vacuole.
questions.answer: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall and a large central vacuole, while animal cells lack a cell wall and have small, temporary vacuoles.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is a compound microscope needed to observe cells?
questions.answer: Cells are extremely small, typically measured in micrometres, and cannot be seen with the naked eye. A compound microscope uses multiple lenses to magnify the image sufficiently for observation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is curd formed when a small amount of existing curd is added to warm milk?
questions.answer: The existing curd contains live Lactobacillus bacteria. When added to warm milk, these bacteria multiply and ferment the lactose in milk into lactic acid, which causes the milk to coagulate and form curd.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do we observe more fungal growth on clothes during the rainy season?
questions.answer: During the rainy season, the humidity is high, which provides a moist environment ideal for fungal spores to germinate and grow. Fungi thrive in damp conditions and feed on organic materials like cotton in clothes.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are antibiotics not effective against viral diseases like the common cold?
questions.answer: Antibiotics target specific structures or processes in bacteria, such as cell wall synthesis or protein production. Viruses lack these structures and use the host cell’s machinery to replicate, so antibiotics have no effect on them.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Cell
questions.answer: A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of a living organism, capable of carrying out all life processes independently.

questions.text: Micro-organism
questions.answer: A micro-organism is a living organism that is too small to be seen with the naked eye and can only be observed using a microscope.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Fermentation
questions.answer: Fermentation is an anaerobic biochemical process in which microorganisms convert sugars into acids, gases, or alcohol, releasing energy in the absence of oxygen.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State three differences between the following.
questions.text: Plant cell and animal cell
questions.answer: Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, while animal cells lack a cell wall. Plant cells contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis, which are absent in animal cells. Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole, whereas animal cells have many small vacuoles.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State three differences between the following.
questions.text: Prokaryotic cell and eukaryotic cell
questions.answer: Prokaryotic cells lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, while eukaryotic cells have a well-defined nucleus and organelles like mitochondria and chloroplasts. Prokaryotes are generally smaller and simpler in structure, found in bacteria and archaea. Eukaryotes are larger and more complex, found in plants, animals, fungi, and protists.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how microorganisms are useful in the environment.
questions.answer: Microorganisms play a vital role in maintaining environmental balance. They decompose dead organic matter like fallen leaves, animal waste, and garbage, converting them into simple substances that enrich the soil. This process, called decomposition, helps in nutrient cycling. Some bacteria in the soil fix atmospheric nitrogen, making it available to plants. Microorganisms are also used in sewage treatment plants to break down harmful organic pollutants. Thus, they help keep the environment clean and fertile.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why food gets spoiled and how we can prevent it.
questions.answer: Food gets spoiled when microorganisms like bacteria, fungi, or yeast grow on it and break down its nutrients, producing unpleasant smells, tastes, or toxic substances. This happens especially in warm, moist conditions. To prevent spoilage, food should be stored in cool, dry places or refrigerated to slow microbial growth. Preservatives like salt, sugar, or oil can also inhibit microbial activity. Proper hygiene and covering food prevent contamination.

questions.answer: Voluntary muscles are under conscious control, e.g., biceps in the arm. Involuntary muscles work automatically without our will, e.g., muscles in the stomach and heart.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: List the main parts of the alimentary canal in order.
questions.answer: The main parts of the alimentary canal are: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, and anus.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: What are enzymes? Mention their role in digestion.
questions.answer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions. In digestion, enzymes like amylase, pepsin, and lipase break down carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into simpler substances.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: Why is the liver important in the digestive system?
questions.answer: The liver produces bile, which helps in the digestion and absorption of fats. It also stores glucose and detoxifies harmful substances.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: Why do we feel hardness when we contract our biceps?
questions.answer: When the biceps muscle contracts, it becomes shorter and thicker, which can be felt as a firm bulge under the skin. This hardness is due to the tightening of muscle fibres during contraction.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: Why is the small intestine longer than the large intestine?
questions.answer: The small intestine is longer (about 6m) to provide more surface area and time for digestion and absorption of nutrients. The large intestine is shorter (about 1.5m) as its main role is water absorption and formation of faeces.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: Why should we avoid tobacco for good digestive health?
questions.answer: Tobacco causes inflammation, ulcers, and increases the risk of cancer in the mouth, throat, and digestive tract. It also impairs saliva production and damages the lining of the alimentary canal.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: Describe the process of digestion in the human body from ingestion to egestion.
questions.answer: Digestion begins in the mouth where food is chewed and mixed with saliva containing amylase. It then passes through the pharynx and oesophagus to the stomach, where gastric juice (HCl, pepsin, mucus) breaks down proteins. The food enters the small intestine where bile, pancreatic juice, and intestinal enzymes complete digestion. Nutrients are absorbed into the blood here. Undigested material moves to the large intestine where water is absorbed, and the remaining waste is expelled through the rectum and anus.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: Explain the types of muscles in the human body with their location, function, and nature of movement.
questions.answer: There are three types of muscles: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones, cause voluntary movements, and maintain posture (e.g., limbs). Cardiac muscles are found only in the heart, contract rhythmically and involuntarily to pump blood. Smooth muscles are present in walls of internal organs like stomach, intestine, and blood vessels; they work involuntarily and slowly to carry out functions like peristalsis and blood flow regulation.

questions.instruction: State the difference between the following.

questions.text: Small intestine and Large intestine
questions.answer: The small intestine is longer (about 6m) and is the main site for digestion and absorption of nutrients. The large intestine is shorter (about 1.5m) and mainly absorbs water and forms faeces.

questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: How do muscles work in pairs to produce movement? Give an example.
questions.answer: Muscles work in antagonistic pairs where one contracts while the other relaxes. For example, to bend the elbow, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes. To straighten the arm, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. This coordinated action allows smooth and controlled movement at joints.

questions.subject: Science
questions.chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
questions.text: Why is the heart made of cardiac muscle and not skeletal muscle?
questions.answer: The heart must contract rhythmically and continuously without fatigue, which cardiac muscle is specially adapted for. It is involuntary, autorhythmic, and resistant to fatigue. Skeletal muscle requires nervous stimulation for each contraction and would not sustain the constant pumping action needed for blood circulation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differentiate between physical and chemical changes with two examples each.
questions.answer: In a physical change, no new substance is formed and the change is usually reversible, e.g., melting of ice and boiling of water. In a chemical change, a new substance with different properties is formed and the change is usually irreversible, e.g., burning of wood and rusting of iron.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why we check the expiry date on canned food.
questions.answer: We check the expiry date on canned food to ensure it is safe to consume, as after the expiry date, harmful chemical changes may occur inside the can, leading to spoilage or production of toxic substances.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Give two examples each of useful and harmful changes.
questions.answer: Useful changes: baking bread, cooking food. Harmful changes: rusting of iron, souring of milk.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are periodic and non-periodic changes? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: Periodic changes occur repeatedly after a fixed interval of time, e.g., change of seasons. Non-periodic changes do not occur at regular intervals, e.g., occurrence of an earthquake.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why should an iron article be given a coat of paint?
questions.answer: An iron article should be painted to prevent contact with moisture and air, which causes rusting. Paint acts as a protective layer and increases the life of the article.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why should a wooden article be polished?
questions.answer: Polishing a wooden article protects it from moisture, dust, and insects, and gives it a smooth and shiny appearance, thus increasing its durability.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do copper and brass utensils need to be tinned?
questions.answer: Copper and brass utensils are tinned to prevent their reaction with acidic foods, which can form toxic compounds; tinning provides a safe, non-reactive coating.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the activity to show that heating sugar leads to a chemical change. Include aim, procedure, observation, and conclusion.
questions.answer: Aim: To show that heating sugar brings about a chemical change. Procedure: Take sugar in an evaporating dish, heat it on a tripod burner, and observe. Observation: Sugar first melts, then turns brown, and finally a blackish substance (carbon) forms at the bottom, with a burnt smell. Conclusion: Since new substances (carbon and water vapour) are formed with different properties and the change is irreversible, it is a chemical change.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the difference between natural and man-made changes with examples. Also classify them as useful and harmful.
questions.answer: Natural changes occur without human intervention, e.g., ripening of fruit, raining. Man-made changes are brought by humans, e.g., baking bread, cutting wood. Useful changes benefit us, e.g., cooking food, sharpening pencil. Harmful changes cause damage, e.g., rusting of iron, spoiling of milk. Some natural changes can be harmful (e.g., flood), and some man-made changes useful (e.g., medicine).

questions.answer: Periodic changes occur repeatedly after a fixed interval of time, e.g., swinging of a pendulum. Non-periodic changes do not occur at regular intervals and their recurrence is unpredictable, e.g., occurrence of an earthquake or lightning.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how melting and boiling of water are physical changes.
questions.answer: Melting and boiling of water are physical changes because only the state of water changes from solid to liquid or liquid to gas, but its chemical composition (H₂O) remains the same. No new substance is formed during these processes. The changes are reversible — water vapour can be condensed back to liquid, and ice can be melted and frozen again. The process involves absorption of heat, but there is no alteration in the molecular structure of water. Hence, they are classified as physical changes.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why rusting of iron is considered a chemical change.
questions.answer: Rusting of iron is a chemical change because iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form a new substance called iron oxide (rust), which has different properties like colour, texture, and strength. The original iron cannot be obtained back from rust by simple physical means. The change is irreversible and occurs slowly in the presence of air and water. Since a new substance with different chemical properties is formed, it is classified as a chemical change.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: If 50 g of sugar is heated and it produces 30 g of carbon and some water vapour, what is the mass of water vapour produced? (Assume no loss of mass.)
questions.answer: Mass of sugar = 50 g Mass of carbon produced = 30 g Let mass of water vapour = x g According to law of conservation of mass: Mass of reactants = Mass of products 50 = 30 + x x = 50 – 30 = 20 g Therefore, mass of water vapour produced = 20 g.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A candle of mass 100 g is burnt completely. After burning, 20 g of solid residue is left. What is the mass of gases produced during burning?
questions.answer: Initial mass of candle = 100 g Mass of residue after burning = 20 g Mass of gases produced = Initial mass – Residue mass = 100 g – 20 g = 80 g Hence, mass of gases produced = 80 g.

questions.answer: An element consists of only one type of atom, e.g., oxygen (O₂). A compound consists of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion, e.g., water (H₂O). Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means, while compounds can.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why chromatography can separate different colours in ink.
questions.answer: Chromatography separates components based on their solubility in the solvent and their adsorption to the stationary phase. Different coloured inks have different solubilities and affinities for the filter paper, so they rise to different heights, appearing as separate spots.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: List two methods to separate insoluble solids from liquids and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Filtration separates insoluble solids like chalk powder from water. Centrifugation separates tiny solid particles like cream from milk by rapid rotation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is an alloy? Give two examples.
questions.answer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, fused together. Examples: brass (copper and zinc) and steel (iron and carbon).

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does the water level not overflow when ice melts in a glass of water?
questions.answer: Ice floats because it is less dense than water. When it melts, the volume of water produced equals the volume of water displaced by the ice, so the water level remains the same.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is a separating funnel used to separate kerosene and water?
questions.answer: Kerosene and water are immiscible liquids with different densities. Water, being denser, settles at the bottom, while kerosene floats on top, allowing separation via the stopcock.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is distilled water used in laboratories?
questions.answer: Distilled water is free from dissolved salts and impurities, making it pure and suitable for accurate experimental results without contamination.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the process of distillation with a labelled diagram. Explain how it helps in obtaining pure water from salt water.
questions.answer: Distillation involves heating salt water in a round-bottom flask to produce vapour. The vapour travels through a condenser where it cools and turns back into liquid water, collected in a conical flask. Salt, being non-volatile, remains behind in the flask. This process separates water from dissolved salts based on the difference in boiling points, yielding pure water.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the difference between elements, compounds, and mixtures. Give two examples of each and state one property that distinguishes them.
questions.answer: Elements are pure substances made of one type of atom (e.g., hydrogen, gold). Compounds are pure substances formed by chemical combination of elements in fixed ratio (e.g., water, carbon dioxide). Mixtures are physical combinations of substances without chemical bonding, with variable composition (e.g., air, soil). Elements and compounds have fixed properties; mixtures show varying properties based on composition. Elements cannot be split chemically; compounds can be broken into elements; mixtures can be separated by physical means.

questions.answer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements chemically combine in a fixed proportion by mass.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Element and Compound
questions.answer: 1. An element consists of only one type of atom; a compound consists of two or more types of atoms chemically bonded. 2. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical methods; compounds can be decomposed into their constituent elements. 3. Elements have uniform composition throughout; compounds also have fixed composition but different from their constituent elements. 4. Example of element: iron; example of compound: rust (iron oxide).

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Mixture
questions.answer: 1. In a homogeneous mixture, components are uniformly distributed; in heterogeneous, they are not. 2. Homogeneous mixtures have only one phase; heterogeneous mixtures show visible phases or particles. 3. Examples of homogeneous: salt solution, air; examples of heterogeneous: sand in water, oil and water. 4. Homogeneous mixtures cannot be separated by filtration; heterogeneous mixtures often can be.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the properties of a compound differ from those of its constituent elements, using water as an example.
questions.answer: Water is a compound made of hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen is a flammable gas, and oxygen supports combustion. However, water is a liquid at room temperature and is used to extinguish fire. This shows that the properties of a compound are entirely different from those of its constituent elements. The chemical bond in water gives it new characteristics not seen in hydrogen or oxygen alone.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why centrifugation is used to separate cream from milk, and not filtration.
questions.answer: Cream particles in milk are very small and light, remaining suspended in the liquid. Filtration cannot separate them because they pass through filter pores. Centrifugation applies centrifugal force that pushes denser milk outward and lighter cream inward, causing cream to collect at the centre or top. This allows effective separation based on density differences under high-speed rotation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A student heats 5.4 g of water and observes that it turns into steam. If the molecular weight of water is 18 g/mol, calculate the number of moles of water vapour produced.
questions.answer: Given: Mass of water = 5.4 g Molecular weight of water = 18 g/mol Number of moles = mass / molecular weight = 5.4 / 18 = 0.3 mol Therefore, 0.3 moles of water vapour are produced.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: In a mixture of sand and salt, 8 g of sand and 2 g of salt are present. What is the percentage of salt in the mixture?
questions.answer: Total mass of mixture = 8 g (sand) + 2 g (salt) = 10 g Mass of salt = 2 g Percentage of salt = (mass of salt / total mass) × 100 = (2 / 10) × 100 = 20% Hence, the percentage of salt in the mixture is 20%.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are the important ingredients of a toothpaste, and what is the function of each?
questions.answer: The important ingredients of toothpaste are calcium carbonate and calcium hydrogen phosphate, which remove dirt and polish the teeth. Fluoride is added to prevent tooth decay and strengthen enamel. Some toothpastes also contain flavoring agents and moisturizers.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are the ingredients of cement?
questions.answer: Cement is made from silica (sand), alumina (aluminium oxide), lime (calcium oxide), iron oxide, and magnesia (magnesium oxide). Portland cement, the most common type, consists of about 60% lime, 25% silica, 5% alumina, and the rest iron oxide and gypsum.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How does the use of a detergent help to clean soiled clothes?
questions.answer: Detergent molecules have two ends: one end attracts water and the other attracts oil and grease. This allows the detergent to lift oil and dirt from the fabric and suspend it in water, which is then rinsed away.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How will you check with the help of soap powder whether water is hard?
questions.answer: Take a small amount of soap powder and shake it with water in a bottle. If lather forms easily, the water is soft. If little or no lather forms and a scum appears, the water is hard.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are roads nowadays made of concrete?
questions.answer: Roads are made of concrete because it is strong, durable, and can withstand heavy traffic and weather changes. Concrete roads do not develop potholes easily and require less maintenance over time.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does synthetic detergent work better than soap in hard water?
questions.answer: Synthetic detergents do not form scum with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water, unlike soap. Therefore, they retain their cleansing action and lather well even in hard water.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is fluoride added to toothpaste?
questions.answer: Fluoride is added to toothpaste because it strengthens the enamel of teeth and makes them more resistant to acid attacks from bacteria, thus preventing tooth decay.

questions.answer: Concrete is a mixture of cement, water, sand, and gravel that hardens into a strong, durable material used in construction.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State the difference between the following.
questions.text: Natural detergents and man-made detergents
questions.answer: Natural detergents are obtained from plants (e.g., soap nut, soap pod) and contain saponin; they are biodegradable and gentle on skin. Man-made detergents are synthesized from fats or petroleum via chemical processes; they work well in hard water and include soaps and synthetic detergents.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: State the difference between the following.
questions.text: Soap and synthetic detergent
questions.answer: Soap is a sodium or potassium salt of fatty acids, made from natural fats and alkali, and forms scum in hard water. Synthetic detergents are made from petrochemicals, do not form scum in hard water, and have stronger cleansing action.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how soap removes dirt from clothes.
questions.answer: Soap molecules have a hydrophilic head that attracts water and a hydrophobic tail that attracts oil and grease. When soap is added to water, the hydrophobic tails attach to oil particles on clothes, while the hydrophilic heads remain in the water. This forms micelles that trap the oil and dirt. The micelles remain suspended in water and are washed away when rinsed. Thus, soap emulsifies the oil and removes it from the fabric.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the process of making soap in the laboratory.
questions.answer: To make soap, coconut oil is taken in a beaker and sodium hydroxide solution is added slowly while stirring. The mixture is heated and boiled for 10-12 minutes with continuous stirring. Then, a salt solution is added to help the soap precipitate and float on the surface. After cooling, the thick soap is separated, perfume is added, and it is poured into a mould to set. The chemical reaction between fat and alkali produces soap and glycerol.

questions.answer: The lithosphere is the hard crust of the earth made up of land and rocks.

questions.text: Why is coal called a fossil fuel?
questions.answer: Coal is called a fossil fuel because it is formed from the remains of ancient plants buried underground.

questions.text: How do forests help in controlling floods?
questions.answer: Forests help control floods by absorbing rainwater and reducing surface runoff.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how mineral oil is formed.
questions.answer: Mineral oil is formed from the remains of dead sea organisms that sank to the bottom of the sea. Layers of sand and soil accumulated over them, and due to high pressure and temperature over millions of years, these remains were transformed into mineral oil.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: List any three uses of forests.
questions.answer: Forests help reduce the velocity of water flowing over land, prevent soil erosion, and help in the percolation of water into the ground. They also control floods, reduce evaporation, and protect wildlife.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What are the four main ores of iron?
questions.answer: The four main ores of iron are magnetite, haematite, limonite, and siderite.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is natural gas considered an eco-friendly fuel?
questions.answer: Natural gas is considered eco-friendly because it produces less smoke and harmful gases when burnt compared to coal and petroleum. It also leaves minimal residue after combustion.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why are all minerals not ores?
questions.answer: All minerals are not ores because ores are only those minerals that contain a high enough proportion of metal to make its extraction economical. Many minerals contain little or no metal and are not suitable for metal extraction.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why should we prevent the wastage of fuel used for vehicles?
questions.answer: We should prevent the wastage of fuel because fossil fuels like petrol and diesel are limited in supply. Wasting them leads to faster depletion of resources, increases pollution, and raises economic costs due to higher fuel consumption.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the diversity of plants and animals in forests declining?
questions.answer: The diversity of plants and animals in forests is declining due to deforestation for agriculture, urbanization, and industrialization. Illegal logging, forest fires, and climate change also destroy habitats, leading to loss of biodiversity.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the formation of coal.
questions.answer: Millions of years ago, dense forests got buried underground due to natural events like earthquakes or floods. Layers of soil and sand kept depositing over these buried plants. Due to high pressure from the layers above and heat from the earth’s interior, the plant remains slowly underwent chemical changes. This process, called carbonization, transformed the organic matter into coal. Over time, with increasing pressure and heat, peat turned into lignite, then bituminous coal, and finally anthracite, the highest grade of coal. Since coal is formed from ancient plant remains, it is classified as a fossil fuel.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how forests help in maintaining the quality of the environment.
questions.answer: Forests play a vital role in maintaining environmental quality. They absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen during photosynthesis, thus purifying the air. Their roots hold the soil together, preventing erosion. Forests also regulate the water cycle by promoting percolation and reducing surface runoff, which helps prevent floods. They provide shade and reduce evaporation from the soil. Additionally, forests provide habitat to countless species of plants, animals, and microbes, preserving biodiversity. They also act as natural filters, trapping dust and pollutants. Thus, forests are essential for ecological balance and a healthy environment.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define fossil fuel.
questions.answer: Fossil fuels are natural fuels such as coal, petroleum, and natural gas, formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals buried underground and subjected to heat and pressure over millions of years.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define mineral.
questions.answer: A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered atomic structure, found in the earth’s crust.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define ore.
questions.answer: An ore is a naturally occurring mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write the difference between the following.
questions.text: Differentiate between metal minerals and non-metal minerals.
questions.answer: Metal minerals contain metals and are usually lustrous, malleable, and good conductors of heat and electricity (e.g., iron, copper). Non-metal minerals do not contain metals, are often dull or transparent, brittle, and poor conductors (e.g., sulphur, mica). Metal minerals are used in making tools and machines, while non-metal minerals are used in fertilizers, insulation, and chemicals.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write the difference between the following.
questions.text: Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable natural resources with examples.
questions.answer: Renewable resources are those that can be replenished naturally in a short period, such as sunlight, wind, and forests. Non-renewable resources are finite and take millions of years to form, such as coal, petroleum, and minerals. Once exhausted, non-renewable resources cannot be quickly replaced, while renewable resources are sustainable if used wisely.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how mineral oil is extracted and refined.
questions.answer: Mineral oil is extracted by drilling oil wells into underground reservoirs where it is trapped. The crude oil is then pumped out and transported to refineries. In the refinery, it undergoes fractional distillation, where it is heated and separated into different fractions based on boiling points. These fractions include aviation petrol, gasoline, diesel, kerosene, lubricating oil, tar, etc. Each fraction is further processed to remove impurities and obtain useful products.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why we should conserve natural resources.
questions.answer: We should conserve natural resources because many of them, like fossil fuels and minerals, are limited and take millions of years to form. Overuse leads to depletion, environmental degradation, and imbalance in ecosystems. Conservation ensures availability for future generations and reduces pollution. It also helps maintain ecological balance and supports sustainable development. Wise use of resources like forests, water, and soil prevents desertification, loss of biodiversity, and climate change.

questions.subject: Science

questions.text: What is an eclipse?
questions.answer: An eclipse occurs when the Sun, Moon, and Earth come in a straight line, causing one to cast a shadow on another.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how scattering of light helps us see the beam of a laser in water mixed with milk.
questions.answer: When milk is added to water, it becomes turbid due to tiny milk particles. The laser light hits these particles and gets scattered in different directions. Some of these scattered rays reach our eyes, making the beam visible.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the formation of umbra and penumbra when an extended source of light is used.
questions.answer: With an extended source, light comes from multiple points. Some parts of the screen receive light from all parts of the source (bright), some from none (umbra, dark), and some from only part of the source (penumbra, faint). This results in a dark central umbra surrounded by a lighter penumbra.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is it dangerous to look at a solar eclipse with the naked eye?
questions.answer: During a solar eclipse, the sun's intense visible and ultraviolet rays are still emitted from the uncovered parts. These rays can damage the retina of the eye, leading to permanent blindness. Special protective goggles are required to filter out harmful radiation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is zero shadow day and where can it be experienced?
questions.answer: Zero shadow day is when the sun is exactly overhead at noon, causing vertical objects to cast no shadow. It occurs only between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, during summer, on different dates depending on latitude.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the sky dark in space beyond Earth’s atmosphere?
questions.answer: The sky appears dark in space because there are no air molecules or particles to scatter sunlight. Without scattering, light travels in straight lines and only reaches the eye when coming directly from a light source like the sun or stars.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does the sun appear red during sunset?
questions.answer: At sunset, sunlight travels through a longer path in the atmosphere. During this longer journey, blue light is scattered out in all directions, while red light, being scattered less, continues straight and reaches our eyes, making the sun appear red.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is a laser beam not visible in clean water but visible when milk is added?
questions.answer: Clean water has no particles to scatter the laser light, so the beam remains invisible from the side. When milk is added, its tiny fat and protein particles scatter the light, making the beam visible as scattered light reaches our eyes.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write a short paragraph in 6-8 lines.
questions.text: Explain the formation of shadows by a point source and an extended source, mentioning umbra and penumbra.
questions.answer: A point source produces a sharp shadow with only an umbra, where no light reaches, and no penumbra. An extended source, being larger, casts a shadow with two parts: a central dark umbra where no light from any part of the source reaches, and a surrounding faint penumbra where light from some parts of the source reaches. The penumbra is fainter because it receives partial illumination. As the screen moves farther, both umbra and penumbra grow larger with an extended source, but with a point source, only the umbra size changes proportionally.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write a short paragraph in 6-8 lines.
questions.text: Describe the scattering of light and its role in natural phenomena like the colour of the sky and the appearance of the sun at sunrise and sunset.
questions.answer: Scattering of light is the deflection of light rays by tiny particles in the atmosphere. Shorter wavelengths like blue are scattered more than longer wavelengths like red. This makes the sky appear blue during the day. At sunrise and sunset, sunlight passes through a thicker layer of atmosphere, causing most of the blue light to be scattered away. The remaining light, rich in red and orange, reaches our eyes, making the sun and sky appear red or orange. This same principle explains why distant mountains appear bluish.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Scattering of light
questions.answer: Scattering of light is the process in which light rays are deflected in different directions when they encounter tiny particles or molecules in their path, making the beam visible from the side.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Umbra
questions.answer: Umbra is the darkest part of a shadow where no light from the source reaches due to complete obstruction by the object.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Penumbra
questions.answer: Penumbra is the faint, partially shaded region surrounding the umbra where light from part of the source reaches, resulting in partial illumination.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Point source and extended source of light
questions.answer: A point source is a tiny light source that emits light from a single point, producing a sharp shadow with only umbra. An extended source has a noticeable size, producing a shadow with both umbra and penumbra. The umbra from a point source is sharper and darker, while from an extended source it may be fainter if the source is large. With an extended source, the penumbra region shows gradual transition from light to dark, absent in point source shadows.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Umbra and penumbra
questions.answer: Umbra is the central, darkest part of a shadow where no light reaches. Penumbra is the outer, lighter part where partial light reaches. Umbra is formed when the object completely blocks the light source, while penumbra occurs due to partial blocking. The size of umbra decreases with distance for a small object, while penumbra increases. Umbra has uniform darkness, penumbra shows a gradient of brightness.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why the sky appears blue during the day and red at sunset using the concept of scattering of light.
questions.answer: The sky appears blue because molecules in the atmosphere scatter shorter wavelengths of light (blue) more effectively than longer wavelengths. This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions, making the sky look blue. At sunset, sunlight travels through a longer path in the atmosphere. As a result, most of the blue light is scattered out of the line of sight before reaching us. The longer wavelengths like red and orange are scattered less and dominate the direct light that reaches our eyes, making the sun appear red.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the distance of the screen affects the size of umbra and penumbra in the shadow of an object illuminated by an extended source.
questions.answer: As the screen is moved farther away from the object, both the umbra and penumbra become larger in size. This happens because the diverging light rays from the extended source spread out more over distance, increasing the area where light is partially or completely blocked. The umbra grows as the region of total darkness expands, and the penumbra widens as the zone of partial illumination spreads. However, if the object is larger than the source, the umbra may eventually disappear at a certain distance. The rate of increase depends on the size of the source and the object.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A student observes that a laser beam is not visible in clean water but becomes visible when 5 drops of milk are added to 100 mL of water. If each drop of milk scatters light effectively and the visibility increases with the number of drops, how would the visibility of the beam change if 10 drops are added instead of 5? Explain.
questions.answer: The visibility of the laser beam increases with the number of milk drops because more particles are available to scatter the light. With 5 drops, a certain number of particles scatter the beam, making it visible. Doubling the number of drops to 10 approximately doubles the number of scattering particles, assuming uniform distribution. This increases the intensity of scattered light in all directions, making the beam appear brighter and more visible from the sides. However, beyond a certain point, too many drops may make the solution too turbid, blocking the beam rather than scattering it. So, visibility increases up to an optimal point, after which it may decrease.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: On zero shadow day, a vertical stick of height 1.5 m casts no shadow at noon. If the same stick is placed at a location where the sun is at an angle of 30° to the vertical, what will be the length of its shadow? Use the formula: shadow length = height × tan(angle from vertical).
questions.answer: Given: height = 1.5 m, angle from vertical = 30°. Shadow length = 1.5 × tan(30°). We know tan(30°) = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577. So, shadow length = 1.5 × 0.577 ≈ 0.866 m. Therefore, the length of the shadow is approximately 0.87 metres.

questions.answer: Oscillatory motion is the to-and-fro motion of an object about its mean position.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How is sound produced?
questions.answer: Sound is produced due to the vibration of an object.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is the relationship between frequency and pitch?
questions.answer: Pitch of sound increases with an increase in frequency.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is amplitude of vibration?
questions.answer: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its mean position.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is the audible frequency range for humans?
questions.answer: The audible frequency range for humans is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the length of a pendulum affects its time period.
questions.answer: The time period of a pendulum increases with an increase in its length. A longer pendulum takes more time to complete one oscillation, while a shorter pendulum oscillates faster. This is because the restoring force acts over a longer arc in a longer pendulum.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How does amplitude affect the loudness of sound? Give an example.
questions.answer: Loudness of sound is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude of vibration. If the amplitude is doubled, the loudness becomes four times greater. For example, striking a drum harder produces a louder sound due to larger amplitude.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differentiate between infrasonic and ultrasonic sounds.
questions.answer: Infrasonic sounds have frequencies below 20 Hz and cannot be heard by humans, e.g., vibrations from earthquakes. Ultrasonic sounds have frequencies above 20,000 Hz and are also inaudible to humans, e.g., used in medical imaging. Both are outside the human audible range.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is a medium necessary for the propagation of sound?
questions.answer: Sound travels as a mechanical wave that requires particle-to-particle interaction to transfer energy. In a vacuum, there are no particles to vibrate and propagate the wave, so sound cannot travel. Hence, a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) is essential.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does a pendulum continue to oscillate for some time before coming to rest?
questions.answer: A pendulum continues to oscillate due to inertia and the restoring force of gravity. It comes to rest gradually because of air resistance and friction at the point of suspension, which dissipate energy as heat.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the sound produced by a tuning fork pure and steady?
questions.answer: A tuning fork produces sound with a single frequency because its prongs vibrate in a simple harmonic motion. The design ensures minimal energy loss and uniform elasticity, resulting in a steady and pure tone.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do we put our ear to the railway track to hear a distant train?
questions.answer: Sound travels faster and with less energy loss in solids like steel compared to air. The railway track conducts the vibrations from the train’s movement efficiently, allowing us to hear the train earlier through the track than through air.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define amplitude of oscillation.
questions.answer: Amplitude of oscillation is the maximum displacement of the oscillating body from its mean position.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define frequency of oscillation.
questions.answer: Frequency of oscillation is the number of complete oscillations made by an oscillator in one second.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define time period of oscillation.
questions.answer: Time period of oscillation is the time taken to complete one full oscillation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write the difference between the following.
questions.text: Difference between loudness and pitch of sound.
questions.answer: Loudness depends on the amplitude of vibration and determines how soft or loud a sound is; pitch depends on the frequency and determines how shrill or flat a sound is. Loudness is related to energy, while pitch is related to the rate of vibration.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write the difference between the following.
questions.text: Difference between oscillatory motion and linear motion.
questions.answer: Oscillatory motion is the to-and-fro movement about a mean position, repeating periodically, while linear motion is movement in a straight line without repetition. Oscillatory motion involves restoring force, whereas linear motion may be uniform or accelerated.

questions.answer: Labels: Mean position (A), Extreme positions (B and C), Amplitude (AB or AC), Length of pendulum (from support to bob), Bob, String, Support point.

questions.answer: Labels: Stretched string, Two fixed ends, Point of pluck, Direction of vibration (arrows), Tension (T), Length (L), Nodes at ends, Antinode in middle.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the pitch of sound produced by a stretched string can be changed.
questions.answer: The pitch of sound from a stretched string depends on its frequency, which can be altered by changing the tension, length, or thickness of the string. Increasing the tension increases the frequency, producing a higher pitch. Decreasing the length (by pressing the string) also increases frequency and pitch. Using a thinner string increases frequency, while a thicker string lowers it. These principles are used in tuning instruments like sitar or guitar.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how intensity of sound is related to the amplitude of vibration.
questions.answer: The intensity of sound is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude of vibration. This means if the amplitude is doubled, the intensity becomes four times greater. Greater amplitude means more energetic vibrations, which transfer more energy to the medium per second. This results in a louder sound perceived by the ear. For example, beating a drum harder increases amplitude and thus loudness significantly.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A pendulum completes 20 oscillations in 16 seconds. Calculate its time period and frequency.
questions.answer: Time for 20 oscillations = 16 s Time for 1 oscillation (T) = 16 / 20 = 0.8 s Frequency (f) = 1 / T = 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 Hz Answer: Time period = 0.8 s, Frequency = 1.25 Hz

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: The frequency of a sound wave is 512 Hz. What is its time period?
questions.answer: Time period (T) = 1 / frequency T = 1 / 512 = 0.001953125 s ≈ 0.002 s Answer: Time period = 0.002 s

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe an activity to show that sound is produced due to vibration of objects. Include the materials used, procedure, observation, and conclusion.
questions.answer: Take a tuning fork and strike it gently against a rubber pad. Bring it near a hanging ping-pong ball. The ball gets kicked away as the tuning fork vibrates. This shows that the tuning fork is vibrating. Now, touch the tuning fork to a bowl of water; ripples are formed, indicating vibration. When the tuning fork stops vibrating, no sound is heard and no disturbance is seen in water. Thus, sound is produced only when the object vibrates. Conclusion: Vibration of an object is necessary for sound production.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the concepts of infrasonic, audible, and ultrasonic sounds with examples and their frequency ranges.
questions.answer: Sounds are classified based on frequency. Infrasonic sounds have frequency below 20 Hz; examples include vibrations from earthquakes, elephant calls, and whale sounds. Audible sounds range from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, which humans can hear, such as speech, music, and everyday noises. Ultrasonic sounds have frequency above 20,000 Hz; examples include bat echolocation, dog whistles, and medical ultrasound. Humans cannot hear ultrasonic or infrasonic sounds, but some animals can. These sounds have various applications in science and technology.

questions.answer: Conduction – it is not a property or behavior of magnetic poles; the others are related to magnetic interactions.

questions.answer: Electromagnet

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does a freely suspended magnet always come to rest in the north-south direction?
questions.answer: Because the Earth acts as a giant magnet and its magnetic south pole attracts the north pole of the suspended magnet.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is meant by magnetic field?
questions.answer: The region around a magnet where its magnetic force can be experienced is called a magnetic field.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: State one use of an electromagnet in daily life.
questions.answer: Electromagnets are used in electric bells and cranes to lift heavy iron loads.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is repulsion considered the sure test for a magnet?
questions.answer: Repulsion occurs only between like poles of two magnets, so observing repulsion confirms both objects are magnets.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What happens to the intensity of a magnetic field as you move away from the magnet?
questions.answer: The intensity of the magnetic field decreases with distance from the magnet.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the single touch method of magnetising a steel bar.
questions.answer: In the single touch method, a bar magnet is dragged repeatedly from one end to the other of a steel bar in the same direction. This process aligns the magnetic domains in the steel bar, inducing magnetism. However, the magnetism produced is weak and temporary.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how magnetic lines of force show the direction and strength of a magnetic field.
questions.answer: Magnetic lines of force emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole of a magnet, showing the direction of the field. The closeness of the lines indicates the strength: closer lines mean a stronger field, while sparse lines indicate a weaker field.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is the penetrating ability of a magnetic field? Give one example.
questions.answer: A magnetic field can pass through non-magnetic materials like cardboard, wood, and water without being blocked. For example, a magnet can attract iron pins even when a cardboard sheet is placed between them.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Differentiate between a permanent magnet and an electromagnet.
questions.answer: A permanent magnet retains its magnetism without external influence, while an electromagnet shows magnetism only when electric current flows through its coil. The strength of an electromagnet can be adjusted by changing the current or number of coils, unlike a permanent magnet.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do magnetic lines of force never intersect each other?
questions.answer: If magnetic lines of force intersected, it would imply two different directions of the magnetic field at the same point, which is impossible. The magnetic field at any point has a unique direction, so lines of force cannot cross.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why does a magnet attract iron pins even when they are not touching?
questions.answer: A magnet exerts a magnetic force that extends into the space around it, forming a magnetic field. This field can exert force on magnetic materials like iron without physical contact, so the pins are attracted from a distance.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the double-touch method preferred over the single-touch method for making strong magnets?
questions.answer: The double-touch method uses two magnets with opposite poles starting from the centre and moving outwards, which aligns the magnetic domains more uniformly and effectively. This results in stronger and longer-lasting magnetism compared to the single-touch method.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the experiment to show the magnetic field around a bar magnet using iron filings. What do you observe and what do you conclude?
questions.answer: Place a bar magnet at the centre of a cardboard sheet. Sprinkle iron filings evenly around it. Gently tap the cardboard. The iron filings arrange themselves in curved lines from the north pole to the south pole of the magnet. These lines are denser near the poles and spread out towards the middle. This shows that magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole, and the field is strongest near the poles where the lines are closest.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the Earth behaves like a giant magnet and how this affects a freely suspended magnet.
questions.answer: The Earth behaves like a giant magnet with its magnetic south pole near the geographic north and magnetic north pole near the geographic south. A freely suspended magnet aligns itself with the Earth’s magnetic field, so its north pole points toward the Earth’s magnetic south, which is near the geographic north. This is why a compass needle always points north-south. William Gilbert concluded this after experimenting with a spherical magnet, showing that the Earth’s magnetism causes the alignment.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Magnetic field
questions.answer: The region around a magnet where its magnetic force can be experienced by another magnetic material is called a magnetic field.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Electromagnet
questions.answer: A temporary magnet made by winding a coil of insulated wire around a soft iron core and passing electric current through it is called an electromagnet.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Magnetic lines of force
questions.answer: Imaginary lines representing the direction and strength of a magnetic field, emerging from the north pole and entering the south pole of a magnet, are called magnetic lines of force.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Single touch method and Double touch method of magnetisation
questions.answer: Single touch method uses one magnet dragged from one end to the other; double touch method uses two magnets with opposite poles starting from the centre and moving outwards. Single touch produces weak and temporary magnetism; double touch produces stronger and more lasting magnetism. In single touch, the magnet is lifted and dragged back; in double touch, both poles move simultaneously without lifting. The double touch method aligns domains more uniformly.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Write 3-4 points of difference between the following.
questions.text: Magnetic force and Gravitational force
questions.answer: Magnetic force acts only on magnetic materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt; gravitational force acts on all objects with mass. Magnetic force can be attractive or repulsive; gravitational force is always attractive. Magnetic force depends on the material and alignment of poles; gravitational force depends on mass and distance. Magnetic force can be shielded; gravitational force cannot be blocked by any material.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Draw a labelled diagram of the following.
questions.text: Draw a labelled diagram showing the magnetic field around a bar magnet using magnetic lines of force.
questions.answer: Bar magnet labelled with N and S poles, curved lines emerging from N pole and entering S pole, lines closer near poles and farther apart at centre, arrows showing direction from N to S.

questions.subject: Science

questions.text: Draw a labelled diagram of a compass showing a magnetic needle and directions.
questions.answer: Circular box with glass cover, magnetic needle free to rotate, needle aligned north-south, labelled N, S, E, W on the base, needle marked with N pole (often coloured).

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how the properties of magnetic lines of force help in understanding the attraction between unlike poles and repulsion between like poles.
questions.answer: Unlike poles attract because the magnetic lines of force between them are in a state of tension, like a stretched spring, pulling the poles together. Like poles repel because the lines of force between them push outward, trying to separate. The lines never intersect and tend to contract longitudinally while expanding laterally. These properties, proposed by Faraday, explain how magnetic forces act at a distance through the field.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain why the intensity of a magnetic field is stronger at the poles than at the centre of a magnet.
questions.answer: The intensity of a magnetic field is stronger at the poles because the magnetic lines of force are most concentrated there, as they emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole. At the centre of the magnet, the lines are spread out and farther apart, indicating a weaker field. The number of lines passing through a unit area perpendicular to the field determines the intensity. Hence, where lines are dense (poles), the field is strong; where they are sparse (centre), the field is weak.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: A student magnetises a steel bar using the single touch method. After 10 strokes, the bar attracts 5 iron pins. After 30 strokes, it attracts 15 pins. If the number of pins attracted is directly proportional to the number of strokes, how many pins will it attract after 50 strokes?
questions.answer: Given: Number of pins attracted ∝ Number of strokes Let pins = k × strokes From 30 strokes → 15 pins: 15 = k × 30 → k = 15/30 = 0.5 For 50 strokes: pins = 0.5 × 50 = 25 Answer: 25 pins

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: Solve the following problem with proper steps.
questions.text: In an experiment, the number of magnetic lines of force passing through a 2 cm² area is 40. If the area is reduced to 1 cm², keeping the same field intensity, how many lines of force will pass through the smaller area?
questions.answer: Field intensity = Number of lines / Area Initial intensity = 40 lines / 2 cm² = 20 lines/cm² Since intensity remains same, for 1 cm²: Lines = intensity × area = 20 × 1 = 20 lines Answer: 20 lines

questions.answer: A nebula is a cloud made up mainly of hydrogen gas and dust particles.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define the horizon.
questions.answer: The horizon is the line at which the sky seems to touch the ground.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is space?
questions.answer: Space is the continuous, empty region between the spheres like planets and stars.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What is the apparent motion of the sun?
questions.answer: The perception of the sun moving across the sky due to the earth's rotation and revolution is its apparent motion.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do stars rise and set?
questions.answer: Stars appear to rise and set because the earth rotates from west to east.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the formation of a star.
questions.answer: Stars are born from nebulae. Gravity attracts gas and dust particles, causing the cloud to contract and become dense. Pressure increases at the core, raising the temperature and starting energy generation, forming a star.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: What precautions should be taken for sky watching?
questions.answer: Sky watching should be done away from city lights, preferably on a new moon night. Use binoculars or telescopes and use the Pole Star as a reference point.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: How is a nakshatra defined?
questions.answer: A nakshatra is the portion of the sky traversed by the moon in one day. The 360-degree path is divided into 27 parts, each being about 13 degrees and 20 minutes.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the role of Saptarshi in locating the Pole Star.
questions.answer: Saptarshi is a kite-shaped constellation. By extending one side of its quadrangle, one can reach the Pole Star, making it a useful reference point.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is the Pole Star important for sky watching?
questions.answer: The Pole Star is located in the north and remains relatively fixed in the sky. It serves as a reliable reference point to identify other constellations and directions.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why do we say the sun enters a particular zodiac sign?
questions.answer: As the earth revolves around the sun, the sun appears to move against the background of different constellations. When a specific constellation is behind the sun, we say the sun has entered that zodiac sign.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Why is it an unnecessary waste to believe that stars influence human life?
questions.answer: Science has proven that celestial bodies like planets and stars do not influence human life. Relying on disproven beliefs wastes time, energy, and money, and one should instead adopt a scientific frame of mind.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Write a paragraph on the lifecycle of stars.
questions.answer: Stars originate from nebulae, which are clouds of hydrogen gas and dust. Gravity causes these clouds to contract, increasing core pressure and temperature until energy generation begins. Over a long period, stars undergo changes like contraction and expansion, which constitute their lifecycle. Depending on their mass, stars may evolve into red giants, supernovas, or black holes, eventually ending their cycle.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Describe the concept of the celestial sphere.
questions.answer: The celestial sphere is a virtual sphere surrounding the earth. When we look into the distance, the sky appears to touch the ground at the horizon, forming a circle. Looking up, the sky appears as a sphere based on this horizon. Key points on this sphere include the zenith (directly above), nadir (directly below), celestial poles (extension of earth's axis), and the celestial equator (extension of earth's equator).

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define Constellation.
questions.answer: A group of stars occupying a small portion of the celestial sphere that appear to form specific figures is called a constellation.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define Zodiac Sign (Raashi).
questions.answer: The ecliptic is divided into 12 equal parts, each subtending 30 degrees at the center of the celestial sphere. Each part is called a zodiac sign or raashi.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Define Meridian.
questions.answer: The great circle that passes through both the celestial poles and the observer's zenith and nadir is called a meridian.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Distinguish between Zenith and Nadir.
questions.answer: Zenith is the point on the celestial sphere directly above the observer's head. Nadir is the point on the celestial sphere directly below the observer's feet.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Distinguish between Sky and Space.
questions.answer: Sky is the portion of the atmosphere and beyond visible as a roof from the earth. Space is the continuous, empty region between celestial bodies like planets and stars.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Draw a labelled diagram of the Celestial Sphere showing Zenith, Nadir, and Celestial Poles.
questions.answer: Labels: Celestial Sphere, Zenith, Nadir, Celestial North Pole, Celestial South Pole, Celestial Equator.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Draw a diagram showing the arrangement of Saptarshi and the Pole Star.
questions.answer: Labels: Saptarshi (Great Bear), Quadrangle, Tail, Pole Star (Polaris), Directional line.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain the apparent motion of the sun.
questions.answer: The sun appears to move from east to west because the earth rotates from west to east. Additionally, as the earth revolves around the sun, the sun appears to move along the ecliptic against the background of stars. This motion is not real but perceived due to the earth's movement.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Explain how to identify the Pole Star using Sharmishtha.
questions.answer: Sharmishtha consists of five bright stars in an M-shape. By drawing a perpendicular bisector of the line joining the third and fourth stars of the M, the line points towards the Pole Star. This helps in locating it when Saptarshi is not visible.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: If a star rises at 8:00 PM tonight, at what time will it rise after 30 days?
questions.answer: Stars rise 4 minutes earlier every day. In 30 days, the star will rise 30 * 4 = 120 minutes earlier. 120 minutes is 2 hours. Therefore, it will rise at 6:00 PM.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: Calculate the angular distance of one nakshatra if the 360-degree path is divided into 27 equal parts.
questions.answer: 360 degrees / 27 parts = 13.33 degrees. 0.33 degrees * 60 minutes = 20 minutes. So, each nakshatra is 13 degrees and 20 minutes.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वाळवंटी प्रदेशातील वनस्पतींमध्ये पाण्याचे संशोधन करण्यासाठी मुळे कसे अनुकूलित झालेली आहेत?

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: हिमप्रदेशातील प्राण्यांची त्वचा जाड असली आणि लांब दाट केस असले त्यामुळे त्यांना कोणते फायदे मिळतात?
questions.answer: हिमप्रदेशातील प्राण्यांची त्वचा जाड असली जेणेकरून त्यात पाणी टिकवून ठेवला जातो. लांब दाट केस असले त्यामुळे त्यांचे शरीर तापमान संतुलन राहतो आणि त्यांना थंडीतही तग धरणे शकते.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: जंगलातील मांसाहारी प्राण्यांचे डोळ्यांचे स्थान बाजूस समोर असले त्यामुळे त्यांना कोणते फायदे मिळतात?
questions.answer: जंगलातील मांसाहारी प्राण्यांचे डोळ्यांचे स्थान बाजूस समोर असले त्यामुळे त्यांना दूर अंतरावरील भक्ष्य नजरेस पडते व त्यामुळे त्यांची चाहूळ भक्ष्यास सहजतेने होईल.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वर्गीकरणातील पदानुक्रमाचा महत्त्व कोणता आहे?
questions.answer: वर्गीकरणातील पदानुक्रमाने सजीवांचे गुणधर्मांतील ठळक आणि मूलभूत साम्य व भेद यांच्या आधारे त्यांचे ठळक गट तयार होतात. हे सजीवांचे वर्गीकरण सोपे बनवते व त्यांचे अभ्यास सोपे होतो.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वाळवंटी वनस्पतींमध्ये पाने नसतात किंवा ती खूप बारीक सुईसारखे असतात का?
questions.answer: वाळवंटी वनस्पतींमध्ये पाने नसतात किंवा ती खूप बारीक सुईसारखे असतात जेणेकरून पाण्याचे वाफेच्या रूपात बाहेर टाकणे घटवून जाते. हे पाणी वाफेच्या रूपात बाहेर टाकणे पाण्याचे नुकसान कमी करतो, ज्यामुळे ते वाळवंटी प्रदेशातील उष्ण व शुष्क परिसरात टिकू शकतात.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: हिमप्रदेशातील वनस्पतींमध्ये जाड साली असली का?
questions.answer: हिमप्रदेशातील वनस्पतींमध्ये जाड साली असली जेणेकरून त्यांची जाड साली त्या थंडीतही तग धरणे शकते. हे जाड साली तापमान संतुलन राखण्यास मदत करतो व त्यांना थंडे परिसरात टिकवून ठेवते.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: जंगलातील वनस्पतींमध्ये आधार उंच वाढतो का?
questions.answer: जंगलातील वनस्पतींमध्ये आधार उंच वाढतो जेणेकरून त्यांचे वेली उंच वाढतात व त्यामुळे त्यांना सूर्यप्रकाश मिळवणे सोपे होतो. हे सूर्यप्रकाश मिळवण्यासाठी स्पर्धा करण्यास मदत करतो.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वाळवंटी, हिमप्रदेश व जंगल प्रदेशातील वनस्पतींमध्ये अनुकूलनांची तुलना करा.
questions.answer: वाळवंटी प्रदेशातील वनस्पतींमध्ये पाण्याचे नुकसान घटविण्यासाठी पाने नसतात किंवा बारीक सुईसारखे असतात, मुळे लहान व तंतुमय असतात, खोड मांसल असतात. हिमप्रदेशातील वनस्पतींमध्ये आकार शंकूसारखा असतो, जाड साली असते, बर्फ साचून राहत नाही. जंगल प्रदेशातील वनस्पतींमध्ये आधार उंच वाढतो, वेली उंच वाढतात, सूर्यप्रकाश मिळवण्यासाठी स्पर्धा असते. हे सर्व प्रदेशे विविध परिसरातील अडचणींचा सामना करण्यासाठी विविध अनुकूलन दर्शवतात.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: प्राण्यांचे वर्गीकरण करण्याचे पद्धती व त्याचे महत्त्व सांगा.
questions.answer: प्राण्यांचे वर्गीकरण गुणधर्मांच्या आधारे केला जातो. त्यात कार्ल लिनियसची दूविनाम पद्धती वापरली जाते, जिथे प्रत्येक सजीबाला वैज्ञानिक नाव दिला जातो जिथे पहिली संज्ञा प्रजाती व दुसरी संज्ञा जाती दर्शवते. वर्गीकरणात पदानुक्रम बनवला जातो जिथे राज्य, फाइल, वर्ग, आदेश, कुल, प्रजाती, जाती यांचा क्रम असतो. हे वर्गीकरण सजीवांच्या वैविध्यACHE अभ्यास सोपे बनवते, नावे मानकीकृत होतात, आणि विविध प्रदेशातील सजीवांची तुलना करण्यास मदत करतो.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: अनुकूलन
questions.answer: प्रत्येक सजीव ज्या परिसरात व वातावरणात राहतो, त्याच्याशी जुळवून घेण्यासाठी त्याच्या शरीराच्या अवयवांमध्ये तसेच जीवन जगण्याच्या पद्धतीमध्ये कालानुरूप घडून आलेल्या बदलाला अनुकूलन म्हणतात.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वर्गीकरण
questions.answer: सजीवांचे वर्गीकरण म्हणजे बनस्पती व प्राण्यांचे वर्गीकरण का ब कोणकोणत्या निकषांच्या आधारे केले जाते?

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: दूविनाम पद्धती
questions.answer: प्रत्येक सजीब ओळखण्यासाठी दूविनाम पद्धतीचा अवलंब केला जातो. त्यानुसार प्रत्येक सजीबाला एक बैज्ञानिक नाव देण्यात आले आहे. या नावात दोन संज्ञा आहेत. पहिली संज्ञा प्रजाती दर्शवते, तर दुसरी संज्ञा जाती दर्शवते.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वनस्पतींमध्ये अन्नग्रहणासाठी अनुकूलन कसे झाले?
questions.answer: वनस्पतींमध्ये अन्नग्रहणासाठी अनुकूलन झाले आहेत जसे की परस्पर परपोषी वनस्पतीमध्ये चूषक मुळे असतात जेणेकरून ते आधारक वनस्पतींच्या रसवाहिन्यांपोहोचत पोषकद्रव्ये शोषून घेतात. काही वनस्पतींमध्ये कीटकांचे भक्षण करून नायट्रोजन मिळवते. अशा वनस्पतींमध्ये पाने किंवा फुलांमध्ये अनुकूलन झालेले असते जेणेकरून कीटकांना आकर्षित करा व त्यांना पकडून ठेवा शकतो.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: प्राण्यांमध्ये परिसर साधर्म्यासाठी अनुकूलन कसे झाले?
questions.answer: प्राण्यांमध्ये परिसर साधर्म्यासाठी अनुकूलन झाले आहेत जसे की विविध रंगांचे सरडे ब नाकतोडे आपल्याला सहजरीत्या दिसत नाहीत. वनस्पतींवर, गवतामध्ये अथवा झाडांच्या खोडांबर असताना त्यांच्या शरीराचा रंग त्या ठिकाणच्या रंगाशी मिळताजुळता राहतो. हे परिसर साधर्म्यासाठी अनुकूलन म्हणजे प्राण्यांना त्यांच्या परिसरात लपून राहणे सोपे होतो.

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: खालील प्रश्नांची उत्तर समपूर्ण कामगिरीसह लिहा.
questions.text: एक वाळवंटी वनस्पतीचे खोडा 500 ग्राम पाणी साठवून ठेवतो. त्याची पाने 10 ग्राम पाणी वाफेच्या रूपात प्रत्येक तास खोवते. 5 तासांनंतर त्याच्या खोडात किती पाणी राहील?
questions.answer: प्रारंभिक पाणी = 500 ग्राम प्रति तास पाणी वाफे = 10 ग्राम 5 तासांसाठी वाफलेली पाणी = 10 × 5 = 50 ग्राम शेष पाणी = 500 - 50 = 450 ग्राम उत्तर: 450 ग्राम

questions.subject: Science
questions.instruction: खालील प्रश्नांची उत्तर समपूर्ण कामगिरीसह लिहा.
questions.text: हिमप्रदेशातील एक प्राणींचा शरीर तापमान 35°C आहे. परिसरातील तापमान -10°C आहे. शरीर व परिसरातील तापमानाचा फरक किती आहे?
questions.answer: शरीर तापमान = 35°C परिसरातील तापमान = -10°C फरक = 35 - (-10) = 35 + 10 = 45°C उत्तर: 45°C

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वनस्पतीच्या अवयवांची कार्ये स्पष्ट करा.
questions.answer: वनस्पतीचे अवयव मूळ, खोड, पाने, फुले, फळे व बिया आहेत. मुळे मातीतून पाणी, खनिजे व क्षार शोषून घेतात, आधार देतात व खाद्य पदार्थे संचयित करतात. खोड वाढतो, पानांना आधार देतो, व पाण्याचे वाहक नल्ये असतात. पाने प्रकाश संश्लेषण करतात, ज्यामुळे खाद्य तयार होतो व ऑक्सीजन मिळवते. फुले परागीभवनेसाठी असतात, ज्या फल व बिया निर्माण करते. फळे बिया संरक्षित करतात व पोषण देतात. बिया नवीन वनस्पतीच्या उत्पादनासाठी वापरतात.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: पर्णपत्राचे भाग व त्यांचे कार्य लिहा.
questions.answer: पर्णपत्राचे भाग पर्णपत्र, पर्णधारा, पर्णाग्र, पर्णतल व उपपर्णे आहेत. पर्णपत्र हा पातळ हिरवा भाग आहे जे प्रकाश संश्लेषण करतो. पर्णधारा पर्णपत्राच्या कडेला भाग आहे जे पाण्य व खनिजे वाहतो. पर्णाग्र पर्णपत्राच्या टोकाला आहे. पर्णतल पर्णपत्राचा खोडाशी जोडलेला भाग आहे. उपपर्णे पर्णतलापाशी लहान पानासारखे भाग आहेत जे काही वनस्पतींमध्ये पाहातात.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: पाण्याचे असंगत वर्तन काय आहे? त्याचा फायदा काय होतो?
questions.answer: पाण्याचे असंगत वर्तन म्हणजे 4°C खाली तापमान कमी केल्यास पाण्याची घनता वाढण्याचे बजाय कमी होणे आणि आकारमान वाढणे. यामुळे बर्फ पाण्यावर तरंगते व जलजीवांचे अस्तित्व समुद्रात शीतकालीन कालात राहते.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: मृदेचे परीक्षण केल्याने कोणते गुणधर्म ओळखता येतात?
questions.answer: मृदापरीक्षणामध्ये मातीचा सामू (pH), रंग, पोत, सेंद्रिय पदार्थांचे प्रमाण आणि विद्युतवाहकता ओळखता येतात. यामुळे मृदेची सुपीकता आणि पिकांसाठी योग्यता ओळखली जाते.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वातावरणाचा दाब हवेचा वेगावर कसा परिणाम देतो?
questions.answer: वातावरणाचा दाब जास्त असलेली ठिकाणापासून कमी दाब असलेली ठिकाणी हवा वाहते. हवेचा वेग वाढल्याने त्याचा दाब कमी होतो व उलट.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: पाण्याचे बर्फ होताना त्याचे आकारमान वाढतो का?
questions.answer: पाण्याने बर्फ होताना त्याचे अणू हेक्सागोनल क्रिस्टल संरचनेत व्यवस्थित होतात. यामुळे अणूंमधील जागा वाढते व एकूण आकारमान वाढतो. यामुळे बर्फाची घनता पाण्यापेक्षा कमी होतो.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: मृदेचा सामू 5.5 असल्यास त्याला आम्लयुक्त मृदा कशा म्हणतात?
questions.answer: मृदेचा सामू 5.5 असल्यास ते 6.5 पेक्षा कमी आहे, ज्यामुळे ते आम्लयुक्त मृदा म्हणतात. आम्लयुक्त मृदेत पिकांचे पोषक तत्वे उपलब्ध नाहीत व मृदेची सुपीकता कमी होतो.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: वातावरणाचा दाब सर्व दिशांनी समान असतो का?
questions.answer: वातावरणाचा दाब सर्व दिशांनी समान असतो कारण हवा एक तरल पदार्थ आहे आणि त्याचे कण सर्व दिशांमध्ये स्वतंत्रपणे गडगडत असतात. त्यामुळे सर्व दिशांमध्ये समान दाब exert होतो.

questions.text: रेताड मृदा व चिकण मृदा
questions.answer: रेताड मृदा: वाळूचे मोठे कणे अधिक, पाण्याचा जलद निचरा, जलधारण क्षमता कमी. चिकण मृदा: सूक्ष्म कणे अधिक, पाण्याचा निचरा थांबवते, जलधारण क्षमता जास्त, पिकांसाठी कम योग्य.

questions.subject: Science
questions.text: हवेचा दाब व पाण्याचा दाब
questions.answer: हवेचा दाब: हवेचे वजनामुळे उत्पन्न, वातावरणात समान, उंची वाढल्याने कमी. पाण्याचा दाब: पाण्याचे वजनामुळे उत्पन्न, गहणता वाढल्याने वाढतो, आधारावर जास्त.
